source.summary:
WHY THE AMD FRAME IS SLOW (from reading the code, no benchmarks run). Chrono sources are under /home/harry/chrono/src. The AMD build is commit f54254fa9f, and `git diff` shows its sensor, terrain and body-geometry sources are identical to local HEAD. Its only uncommitted edits are SWIG files that expose the Vulkan classes to Python. AMD's CMakeCache has CH_USE_SENSOR_VULKAN_RT_GPU=ON. The renderer is Mesa 24.2.8 lavapipe (LLVM 19.1). I saved the Mesa files I cite under artifacts/traverse/fdm_f104_50h_20260909/render_latency_v1/source_analysis/mesa-24.2.8/.

1) The whole scene is rebuilt from scratch on almost every frame. On AMD the render runs in full, on the Python thread, inside manager.Update() (chrono_sensor/ChSensorManager.cpp:231-233 → vulkan/ChVulkanRTEngine.cpp:79-121). Each time a frame is due, Chrono fingerprints every body's position and velocity to 1e-8 (vulkan/ChVulkanRTScene.cpp:481-484, 558-571, 610-638). If the fingerprint changed, it re-copies every triangle of every mesh into its own staging list (676-791) before checking whether anything really changed (797). Each copied triangle takes about 576 bytes, including 8 text strings. This scene has about 796,600 triangles:
- terrain: 522,242 (2×511×511, chrono_vehicle/terrain/RigidTerrain.cpp:316)
- HMMWV chassis: 172,563
- 4 rims: 12,381 each
- 4 tires: 13,056 each

Any pose or velocity difference bumps the scene version (801). Even a parked vehicle almost surely has velocity jitter above 1e-8, and velocity is compared too (444-449).

A new scene version makes the renderer (vulkan/ChFilterVulkanRTRender.cpp:2029-2033, 2810-2891) redo everything:
- It moves every triangle into world coordinates and writes one material record per triangle. That is about 153 MB of vertices plus 115 MB of materials.
- It re-uploads 8 buffers, each through a newly allocated staging buffer and its own blocking submit-and-wait (2350-2395).
- It deletes and fully rebuilds a single bottom-level structure holding terrain and vehicle together, plus the top-level structure (2893-3061). There is no refit, no instancing and no split between static and moving geometry.

Lavapipe's builder would ignore a refit request anyway. It never reads the build mode, runs on one thread (lvp_execute.c:4487-4492), and splits triangles purely by the order they were submitted, with no spatial sorting (lvp_acceleration_structure.c:153-179).

2) Only the ray casting runs in parallel. vkCmdTraceRays becomes one software compute job: all shader stages are merged into one JIT-compiled shader (lvp_ray_tracing_pipeline.c:1025-1107) and walk the tree one ray at a time (lvp_nir_ray_tracing.c:385-521). The work is split into LP_NUM_THREADS equal, fixed chunks with no rebalancing (lp_cs_tpool.c:154-155, 57-74). The default thread count is the CPUs the process may run on, capped at 32 (u_cpu_detect.c:752-753, 809; lp_screen.c:1171-1175; lp_limits.h:69). A depth frame casts one ray per pixel (shaders/chrono_sensor_vkrt.rgen:895-899). The Chrono-side restaging, flattening and uploads, and lavapipe's tree build, all run on a single thread.

3) Copying the frame out is cheap. It is a few passes over 4 MB (ChFilterVulkanRTRender.cpp:3215-3254; filters/ChFilterAccess.cpp:576-622; an unused depth-to-greyscale pass in ChFilterImageOps.cpp:200-224). Python gets a zero-copy view and makes one flipped copy (scene.py:204-208).

WHY OPTIX IS FAST LOCALLY. OptiX uploads each mesh and builds its per-mesh structure once, on the first Update (ChOptixEngine.cpp:229-231, 625-743; ChOptixGeometry.cpp:531-554, 595-688). Each frame it only recomputes about 10 instance transforms and rebuilds a tiny top-level structure (ChOptixGeometry.cpp:797-847). It then casts one ray per pixel in hardware on worker threads (ChFilterOptixRender.cpp:51-59; depth_cam_raygen.cu:56-79).

LIKELY PICTURE ON AMD. Each frame is a large, single-threaded, resolution-independent rebuild of the whole world, plus a software ray-casting stage that scales with pixels and threads. The rebuild probably happens even when the vehicle is parked. The slowdown to 4.3-4.6 s with four runs per node fits oversubscription: if each lavapipe instance sees all 16 cores, four runs launch four full thread pools. The source cannot say how the 2.6 s splits between rebuild and ray casting; the benchmark data has to settle that.

BIGGEST LEVER THAT NEEDS NO CHROFORK CHANGE. Render from a separate render-only Chrono system holding just the fixed terrain and the fixed assets. Its fingerprint then never changes, so after the first frame nothing is restaged or rebuilt (ChVulkanRTScene.cpp:690-692), leaving only ray casting and copy-out. Per the sensor_v2 finding in project memory, a vehicle-included frame with the footprint mask applied equals a vehicle-free frame, so the planner input should not change.

cost_centers.name: Per-frame scene fingerprint walk
cost_centers.where: vulkan/ChVulkanRTEngine.cpp:79-104 calls ChVulkanRTScene::SyncFromSystem (vulkan/ChVulkanRTScene.cpp:676-692); fingerprint at 558-638 (every body pointer, pose, velocity, identifier and per-shape material state; values quantised to 1e-8 at 481-489)
cost_centers.per_frame_work: Runs once per Update in which a sensor is due (engine due check at ChVulkanRTEngine.cpp:87-97). Walks all bodies and other physics items and hashes each shape's materials (547-556). A body with an empty visual model still has its pose and velocity hashed (564-571). Vehicle parts switched to NONE keep an empty model, because Clear() does not remove it (chrono_vehicle/ChPart.cpp:475-478).
cost_centers.scales_with: number of bodies, shape instances and materials (not triangles)
cost_centers.significance: Small in itself, but it is the trigger: any pose or velocity change of 1e-8 or more on any body that has a visual model starts the expensive restaging below.

cost_centers.name: CPU restaging of every visual triangle
cost_centers.where: vulkan/ChVulkanRTScene.cpp:694-791 (stage every visible shape), FillTrianglePrimitive 242-364, per-triangle material copy 350-355, compare 797 / 444-475, replace-and-free old list 798-801; per-triangle record layout at ChVulkanRTScene.h:59-115
cost_centers.per_frame_work: Whenever the fingerprint changed, builds a new list of all ~796,600 triangles: 3 vertices, normals, UV tangent maths, and a full material record containing 8 std::string fields, about 576 bytes each (≈459 MB). Then compares it with the old list; if the vehicle moved, this exits at the first primitive. Finally frees the old list. If content really differs, it bumps the scene version (Touch, 801). The whole new list is built before the comparison, so even a no-change frame pays the full copy plus a full triangle-by-triangle compare.
cost_centers.scales_with: total triangles in the scene (terrain 522,242 + vehicle 274,311 + assets); single-threaded on the Python thread; memory-bandwidth and allocator bound
cost_centers.significance: Likely a major resolution-independent share of the 2.6 s. It occurs for moving frames and very probably for parked ones too, because velocities are compared at 1e-8 (448-449). Not measurable from source.

cost_centers.name: Flatten-and-upload of the whole scene (renderer side)
cost_centers.where: vulkan/ChFilterVulkanRTRender.cpp:2029-2033 (rebuild when scene version changed) → BuildScene 2810-2891; AddMesh 2785-2808; AddGpuTriangle 2557-2602; per-triangle material plus 8 texture lookups 2533-2555 / 2397-2434; UploadVector 2350-2395; submit-and-wait 2141-2150
cost_centers.per_frame_work: Moves every triangle into world coordinates with no vertex sharing: 3 vertices × 64 bytes ≈ 153 MB. Writes one 144-byte material record per triangle (≈115 MB), plus ≈22 MB of triangle and index data. Uploads 8 buffers, each through a newly allocated staging buffer (2366-2369) with a separate blocking queue submit and fence wait. On a software device both copies are host RAM, so every byte is copied twice and fresh pages are faulted in each frame. Spheres become 960 triangles and cylinders 128 (2670-2783).
cost_centers.scales_with: total triangles; single-threaded; memory bandwidth, page faults, allocator
cost_centers.significance: Likely a major resolution-independent share. Shared by the depth and RGB cameras (shared renderer 3322-3348), so it is paid once per Update.

cost_centers.name: Acceleration structure delete and full rebuild
cost_centers.where: ChFilterVulkanRTRender.cpp:2893-2982 (one bottom-level structure over all triangles: BUILD mode, PREFER_FAST_TRACE, no ALLOW_UPDATE at 2923-2929; non-opaque when the scene has transparency, 2920), 2984-3061 (top-level structure with one identity instance, 2991-2999); lavapipe lvp_execute.c:4487-4492 → lvp_acceleration_structure.c:264-611
cost_centers.per_frame_work: Destroys the old top- and bottom-level structures and allocates new structure and scratch buffers (2940-2954, 3001-3050). Lavapipe then, single-threaded: zeroes the whole structure (≈83 MB for 796k triangles: 48-byte leaf + 56-byte internal node each, sizes at 55-59, memset at 271); copies 3 vertices per triangle through the index buffer into leaves (343-481); recursively builds a balanced binary tree split at the index midpoint with bottom-up bounding boxes (153-262, 594-595). Then the top-level structure is built again.
cost_centers.scales_with: total triangles (linear); single-threaded; tree quality depends on Chrono's triangle order (vehicle first, then terrain row by row per RigidTerrain.cpp:367-380)
cost_centers.significance: Moderate. Linear-time and simple, but paid every frame together with the uploads, and it cannot be refitted: lavapipe never reads the build mode, and Chrono always requests BUILD.

cost_centers.name: Ray casting on the CPU (depth camera)
cost_centers.where: ChFilterVulkanRTRender.cpp:3156-3213 (vkCmdTraceRaysKHR width×height×1 at 3172, output copy in the same submit, wait at 3212); shaders/chrono_sensor_vkrt.rgen:875-899 (depth: one primary ray per pixel, closest-hit), rchit 47-76; lavapipe dispatch lvp_execute.c:4552-4583 with 8-ray blocks (lvp_ray_tracing_pipeline.c:1036); thread pool lp_state_cs.c:1755-1762, lp_cs_tpool.c:57-74, 154-155; traversal lvp_nir_ray_tracing.c:385-521, box test 61-141, 48-entry stack lvp_ray_tracing_pipeline.c:359
cost_centers.per_frame_work: 1024×1024 ≈ 1.05M rays, one per pixel, no supersampling for depth. Each ray is scalar JIT code walking a two-child tree about 20 levels deep, runs the closest-hit shader (reads vertex, triangle and material buffers) and writes one float. About 30% of rays miss the 80 m arena (stored AMD frame valid fraction 0.70) and stop at the root box. Work goes to LP_NUM_THREADS workers in equal fixed chunks; the calling thread only waits.
cost_centers.scales_with: pixels × tree depth (log2 of triangles) ÷ threads; imbalance between chunks at the image rim vs. centre
cost_centers.significance: The resolution-dependent share and the only part that uses more cores. Its share of the 2.6 s is unknown from source; the size sweep settles it.

cost_centers.name: RGB camera extra ray casting (when enabled)
cost_centers.where: rgen:771-790 (sample_factor² camera rays, default factor 1 per ChCameraSensor.h:79 and scene.py:434), 525-642 (direct lighting: one shadow visibility ray per lit hit, 624-626), 692-712 (mirror ray only if metallic), 134-140 plus ChSensorManager.cpp:52 (up to 7 transparent continuations); transparency flag ChFilterVulkanRTRender.cpp:2548-2553, 2887 and the material-aware shadow loop rgen:402-445
cost_centers.per_frame_work: A second full dispatch with shading: at least 2 rays per lit pixel. The HMMWV chassis materials are partly transparent (data/vehicle/hmmwv/hmmwv_chassis.mtl: Window_Glass d 0.3, Headlight_Lenses d 0.2, BrakeLite_Lenses d 0.85). That flags the whole scene transparent, so shadow rays use the slower up-to-8-trace material-aware loop instead of stopping at the first hit. Also one RGBA8 access copy (ChFilterAccess.cpp:75-106).
cost_centers.significance: Adds roughly one or more ray-casting stages per frame. It does not add a second rebuild (shared renderer). Irrelevant for depth-only runs (nav_runner.py:116-121).

cost_centers.name: Readback and host filter graph
cost_centers.where: ChFilterVulkanRTRender.cpp:3174-3196 (device-to-staging copy), 3215-3254 (memcpy into the host depth buffer, 3230-3232); filters/ChFilterAccess.cpp:576-610 and 622 (copy into a buffer that is freshly allocated each frame, because GetBuffer moves the array out at ChFilterAccess.h:141-150); ChFilterDepthToRGBA8 always attached (sensors/ChDepthCamera.cpp:47-49) and run on the host (filters/ChFilterImageOps.cpp:200-224); Python zero-copy view (chrono_swig/interface/sensor/ChModuleSensor.i:139, ChSensorBuffer.i:170-175) plus one flipped copy (src/nedm/traverse/scene.py:204-208)
cost_centers.per_frame_work: About 5 passes over 4 MB of floats, one new 4 MB allocation, and an unused greyscale image.

cost_centers.name: Blocking synchronisation
cost_centers.where: ChFilterVulkanRTRender.cpp:2141-2150 (vkQueueSubmit plus vkWaitForFences), called from UploadVector 2394, bottom-level build 2978, top-level build 3060, trace 3212; engine applies filters inline at ChVulkanRTEngine.cpp:113-120; scene.py _Tap.take 184-196
cost_centers.per_frame_work: About 11 blocking submit-and-wait cycles per rebuilt frame; everything finishes before Update() returns, so take() returns at once.
cost_centers.significance: Small overhead in itself. It means update_s is essentially the whole render on AMD, while take_s should be about 0.

cost_centers.name: One-time pipeline and device creation
cost_centers.where: ChVulkanRTEngine.cpp:38 (device); ChFilterVulkanRTRender.cpp:2014-2019, 2152-2300 (load 5 SPIR-V modules, vkCreateRayTracingPipelinesKHR at 2278); lavapipe merges all stages into one compute shader and JIT-compiles it (lvp_ray_tracing_pipeline.c:1025-1107); SPIR-V compiled at build time (chrono_sensor/CMakeLists.txt:850-864, GPU path enabled at 979-980); AMD env.sh comment: about 77 s without MESA_SHADER_CACHE_DIR, about 0.8 s with it
cost_centers.per_frame_work: None per frame. Once per renderer, cached per (device, scene) in a process-wide map (3322-3348). A new ChSensorManager or scene pays it again.
cost_centers.scales_with: once per process or scene build; Mesa cache state
cost_centers.significance: First frame only; huge if the cache is cold.

cost_centers.name: Thread oversubscription with co-located runs
cost_centers.where: lavapipe default threads: u_cpu_detect.c:752-753, 809 (CPUs in the affinity mask) → lp_screen.c:1171-1175 (LP_NUM_THREADS override, cap 32 at lp_limits.h:69); fixed chunking lp_cs_tpool.c:154-155
cost_centers.per_frame_work: Each process starts its own pool of up to min(affinity CPUs, 32) ray-casting threads. The chunks are fixed, so an overloaded thread slows its whole chunk.
cost_centers.scales_with: runs per node × threads per run ÷ physical cores
cost_centers.significance: A plausible cause of 2.6 s → 4.3-4.6 s with four runs per 16-core node, if each run's affinity mask covers all cores. The serial rebuild would also slow from memory-bandwidth sharing.

cost_centers.name: OptiX one-time scene construction
cost_centers.where: optix/ChOptixEngine.cpp:229-231 (only when no root exists yet), 625-743; mesh upload deduplicated per mesh (optix/ChOptixPipeline.cpp:975-1034); compacted per-mesh GAS (optix/ChOptixGeometry.cpp:531-554, 595-688); terrain is not mutable (chrono/assets/ChVisualShape.cpp:24) so it takes the rigid path (ChOptixEngine.cpp:669-674); shaders NVRTC-compiled at AddSensor (ChOptixEngine.cpp:181; ChOptixUtils.cpp:74-170)
cost_centers.per_frame_work: None after the first Update. Terrain and vehicle meshes are uploaded and turned into GAS once.
cost_centers.significance: Explains the 8.8 s scene build and 0.044 s first frame measured locally.

cost_centers.name: OptiX per-frame update and hardware ray casting
cost_centers.where: ChOptixEngine.cpp:236-286 (capture body transforms 240 and 268, sensor transforms 765-812), scene thread 422-469 → ChOptixGeometry.cpp:797-847 (recompute 2-key motion transforms for all instances, upload, full IAS BUILD with PREFER_FAST_TRACE and no update flag, device sync); render thread 387-420 → ChFilterOptixRender.cpp:51-59 (optixLaunch W×H); depth_cam_raygen.cu:56-79 (one ray per pixel); DtoH copy ChFilterAccess.cpp:307-326; stream sync ChOptixEngine.cpp:410; Update waits for the render thread when lag has elapsed (292-316)
cost_centers.per_frame_work: Rebuilds a top-level structure over about 10 instances. The meshes are never touched again. Ray casting is in hardware; 4 MB is copied back over PCIe.
cost_centers.significance: About 0.5 ms per frame at 256² locally. There is no whole-world rebuild.

levers.lever: Render from a separate render-only Chrono system that holds only the fixed terrain patch (plus the fixed per-episode assets), with the depth camera attached to that terrain body and the render system's clock advanced before each Update (e.g. SetChTime or one empty step). The physics system keeps the vehicle.
levers.expected_effect: After the first frame the fingerprint never changes, so there is no restaging, no flatten/upload and no tree rebuild. Per-frame cost should fall to the fingerprint walk, ray casting and copy-out. If the rebuild dominates today, this is the biggest single cut, and it needs no Chrono change. The output differs only inside the vehicle footprint, which the planner already masks (project memory: masked vehicle-included frame equals vehicle-free input).
levers.evidence: The renderer walks the manager's system (ChSensorManager.cpp:52-54, 421-422; ChVulkanRTEngine.cpp:104). It returns early when the fingerprint is unchanged (ChVulkanRTScene.cpp:690-692). The renderer rebuilds only when the scene version changes (ChFilterVulkanRTRender.cpp:2029-2033). A fixed body has constant pose and zero velocity in the fingerprint (558-571, 610-626). The due check uses that system's clock (ChVulkanRTEngine.cpp:79-97), and GetBuffer uses the parent body's system time (ChFilterAccess.h:135-141).

levers.lever: Chrono fork fix A: fingerprint only bodies that have visible shapes, and stop hashing and comparing velocities unless a radar sensor is present.
levers.expected_effect: Parked-vehicle frames stop triggering full rebuilds. Frames where the vehicle moved still rebuild. Small, safe code change.
levers.evidence: Velocities are hashed (ChVulkanRTScene.cpp:569-570, 620-625) and compared at 1e-8 (448-449). Bodies with empty models are still hashed (564-571). Velocity is only consumed by radar (ChVulkanRTScene.h:132-135; ChFilterVulkanRTRender.cpp:3686-3696).

levers.lever: Chrono fork fix B: keep one acceleration structure per mesh, built once in the mesh's own coordinates, and rebuild only the top-level structure each frame with updated instance transforms, as OptiX does.
levers.expected_effect: Removes the per-frame flatten, re-upload and tree rebuild of ~797k triangles even while the vehicle drives. The top-level rebuild over about 10 instances is trivial. Per-frame cost becomes ray casting plus a small update. Also avoids relying on lavapipe refit, which does not exist.
levers.evidence: Primitives are already staged in mesh-local coordinates (ChVulkanRTScene.h:123-126) and moved to world space only in AddMesh (ChFilterVulkanRTRender.cpp:2785-2808). A single bottom-level structure is built over everything (2893-2982) with a one-instance identity top level (2984-3061). OptiX builds per-mesh structures once and rebuilds only the top level (ChOptixGeometry.cpp:531-554, 797-847). Lavapipe supports instance nodes with transforms (lvp_acceleration_structure.c:513-550) but never reads the build mode (264-611).

levers.lever: Chrono fork fix C: cut the per-triangle overhead in the Vulkan path: one material table per mesh instead of a 144-byte record per triangle, no 8-string material copy per staged triangle, build the staging list only after a cheap change check, and keep persistent staging buffers.
levers.expected_effect: Shrinks the resolution-independent part roughly in proportion to bytes touched: about 459 MB of staging records plus about 290 MB uploaded twice per rebuild. Useful even before fix B.
levers.evidence: Per-triangle material copy (ChVulkanRTScene.cpp:350-355; record with 8 strings at ChVulkanRTScene.h:59-98, ≈576 bytes per staged triangle). Staging is built before comparing (694-797). Per-triangle GPU material and 8 texture lookups with a string copy (ChFilterVulkanRTRender.cpp:2533-2555, 2400, 2596-2597). New staging buffer per upload (2366-2369).

levers.lever: Drop the HMMWV meshes from the render (visualization NONE plus no roof marker) or use primitive shapes.
levers.expected_effect: Removes 274,311 of ~796,600 triangles (about 34%) from every rebuild and removes the transparent glass that makes the whole scene non-opaque. With NONE and no marker, no triangles on the scene actually move. That should stop GPU rebuilds, but the CPU restage-and-compare of the 522k terrain triangles continues every frame, because the vehicle parts' empty models still change the fingerprint. The separate render system avoids that remaining cost.
levers.evidence: Triangle counts from data/vehicle/hmmwv/*.obj: chassis 172,563; rim 12,381; tire 13,056 (4 each). Meshes are enabled at scene.py:358-360, marker at 370-371. Primitive fallback at chrono/utils/ChBodyGeometry.cpp:227-237. Clear() leaves an empty model (chrono_vehicle/ChPart.cpp:475-478), and empty models still hash pose and velocity (ChVulkanRTScene.cpp:564-571). Transparency flag at ChFilterVulkanRTRender.cpp:2548-2553, 2920.

levers.lever: Set LP_NUM_THREADS to the cores actually allocated to each run and bind each run's CPUs in SLURM (cpus-per-task plus cpu binding), especially when four runs share a 16-core node.
levers.expected_effect: Removes oversubscription in the ray-casting stage; likely recovers much of the 2.6 → 4.3-4.6 s slowdown when runs share a node. Does not speed up the single-threaded rebuild.
levers.evidence: Default thread count is the affinity-mask CPU count, capped at 32 (u_cpu_detect.c:752-753, 809; lp_screen.c:1171-1175; lp_limits.h:69). Fixed equal chunks with no rebalancing (lp_cs_tpool.c:154-155, 57-74). Tree build is serial (lvp_execute.c:4487-4492), and Chrono's staging runs on the Python thread (ChVulkanRTEngine.cpp:104-120).

levers.lever: Render at about 640-768 px instead of 1024 px.
levers.expected_effect: Ray casting and copy-out scale with pixels: 640² is 0.39× and 768² is 0.56× the 1024² cost. The map still gets at least one sample per cell, because the ground footprint is about 95.7 m wide, so each 0.156 m cell needs ≥ ~615 px. No effect on the rebuild share.
levers.evidence: One ray per pixel (rgen:895-899); dispatch grid proportional to width×height (lvp_execute.c:4578-4582); per-pixel copies (ChFilterVulkanRTRender.cpp:3230-3232). The planner grid is 512 cells over 80 m (scripts/sensor_map_v2.py:26-28, back-projection 43-55). Runner camera is 1024² (scripts/nav_online.py:46); stored frame metadata says model_image_size 512.

levers.lever: Use a coarser visual-only terrain mesh (e.g. a 256² heightmap for rendering) while keeping the 512² collision mesh.
levers.expected_effect: While rebuilds persist, terrain triangles drop 4× (522k → 130k), cutting staging, upload and tree build roughly in proportion, and the tree gets 2 levels shallower for ray casting. Costs height fidelity (0.31 m vertex spacing vs 0.156 m).
levers.evidence: Triangle count 2×(W−1)×(H−1) (RigidTerrain.cpp:301-316). AddPatch's heightmap overload has a visualization flag (RigidTerrain.cpp:285-294), so collision and render meshes can differ. All rebuild stages are linear in triangles (ChVulkanRTScene.cpp:284-361; ChFilterVulkanRTRender.cpp:2785-2808; lvp_acceleration_structure.c:343-481).

levers.lever: Keep the RGB camera off for depth-only planners (already the default in nav_runner when checkpoints do not read colour).
levers.expected_effect: Saves the second, heavier ray-casting stage and its copy, but not the rebuild. Expected saving is at least one full ray-casting pass.
levers.evidence: with_rgb switch at scene.py:433-440 and nav_runner.py:116-121. The renderer is shared, so the rebuild happens once per Update (ChFilterVulkanRTRender.cpp:3322-3348, 2029). RGB shading casts shadow rays (rgen:542-626), and the transparency loop is active because of chassis glass (rgen:402-445).

levers.lever: Make sure the Mesa shader cache is warm and readable for every run.
levers.expected_effect: First frame drops from about 77 s to about 0.8 s (per env.sh). No effect on later frames.
levers.evidence: Pipeline created once per renderer (ChFilterVulkanRTRender.cpp:2152-2300, 3322-3348); lavapipe JIT-compiles the merged shader (lvp_ray_tracing_pipeline.c:1025-1107); MESA_SHADER_CACHE_DIR in /work1/dannegrut/harry/nrd/env.sh.

levers.lever: Chrono fork fix D: sort triangles spatially (e.g. Morton order) before handing them to Vulkan, and put static and moving geometry in separate structures.
levers.expected_effect: Better tree quality under lavapipe's index-order builder, so fewer box tests per ray. Mainly helps rays over the vehicle and over the mixed vehicle/terrain branches near the root.
levers.evidence: Lavapipe splits at the index midpoint with no spatial sort (lvp_acceleration_structure.c:163-179). Chrono submits vehicle meshes first and then terrain rows (system body order; RigidTerrain.cpp:170, 367-380; BuildScene order ChFilterVulkanRTRender.cpp:2845-2861).

levers.lever: Minor: remove the always-on depth-to-greyscale filter and reuse the access buffer instead of allocating 4 MB per frame (Chrono change).
levers.expected_effect: A few milliseconds per frame at 1024². Negligible next to the rebuild and ray casting.
levers.evidence: sensors/ChDepthCamera.cpp:47-49; filters/ChFilterImageOps.cpp:200-224; ChFilterAccess.h:147 moves the array out and ChFilterAccess.cpp:595-598 reallocates it; the filter list is locked, so Python cannot remove it (ChVulkanRTEngine.cpp:65-66).

open_questions: How does the 2.6 s split? Fit total = a + b·pixels from depth-only runs at 256/512/1024 on one AMD node. a ≈ the resolution-independent rebuild (restaging, flatten/upload, tree build); b ≈ ray casting plus copy-out. Also confirm take_s ≈ 0 on AMD, since everything should finish inside Update().

Does a parked vehicle still trigger a full rebuild? On AMD, manager.scene is a ChVulkanRTScene with GetRevision() and GetStats() wrapped by the uncommitted ChSceneVulkan.i (declared at ChVulkanRTScene.h:174-176). Log GetRevision() around every Update in the static and moving regimes. Prediction: it increments every frame in both, so static ≈ moving time.

Terrain-only isolation. (a) Same system with vehicle visuals NONE and no marker: expect the version to stop changing but CPU restage-and-compare to continue. (b) Separate render-only system: expect no restaging at all. Compare times of (a), (b) and the full scene. Also compare the depth maps outside the vehicle footprint to confirm they are identical.

LP_NUM_THREADS sweep (1, 2, 4, 8, 16) at 1024 depth-only on an exclusive node: how much speeds up with threads, and how large is the serial remainder? Inside the SLURM job, record os.sched_getaffinity(0) and the lavapipe thread count actually used by default.

Four runs on one node: repeat with LP_NUM_THREADS=4 per run plus CPU binding vs the default, to test whether the 4.3-4.6 s is thread oversubscription or memory-bandwidth contention in the serial rebuild.

Is the lavapipe renderer actually active in every AMD run, or did any node silently fall back to Chrono's own CPU renderer? The fallback message only prints with verbose on (ChVulkanRTEngine.cpp:36-47). Call manager.SetVerbose(True) before AddSensor and look for 'Chrono::Sensor Vulkan RT device: llvmpipe…' (ChVulkanRTDevice.cpp:174-176).

Within the rebuild, how much is Chrono (staging, world-space flattening, 8 staging uploads) vs lavapipe's tree build? This needs a profiler on AMD (perf record/report on the Python process) or wall-clock timing with triangle counts varied (vehicle meshes on/off, 256² vs 512² terrain).

How good is lavapipe's index-order tree for this triangle order? Measure ray-casting time per pixel with and without vehicle meshes, and with a spatially coherent vs shuffled submission order if a fork build is available.

Does the AMD runtime tree contain chrono/data/sensor/textures/grass_texture.jpg under the repo root used by nav_runner? It decides whether every terrain triangle carries a long texture-path string, which adds heap allocations in staging and texture lookup. It does not change depth.

How big is the RGB-on vs RGB-off difference per frame on AMD, and does the chassis glass (non-opaque scene, material-aware shadow loop) make the RGB stage noticeably slower than one extra depth-like pass?
Is the Mesa shader cache warm and hit on every run, and do concurrent runs contend on it? Look at first-frame time per run.

Local cross-check: the local build cannot run the Vulkan depth path, because ChDepthCamera binds to OptiX at compile time (sensors/ChDepthCamera.h:27-35). A separate Vulkan-only build in a new build directory, run on local lavapipe (Mesa 25.2.8 installed) and on the NVIDIA Vulkan driver, would separate Chrono's rebuild cost from lavapipe's ray-casting cost on known hardware.
lavapipe_notes: What AMD runs: /work1/dannegrut/harry/nrd/toolchain/lvp/lib/libvulkan_lvp.so reports 'Mesa 24.2.8' with LLVM 19.1 and contains VK_KHR_ray_tracing_pipeline. The Chrono build has CH_USE_SENSOR_VULKAN_RT_GPU=ON, which compiles the Vulkan renderer (chrono_sensor/CMakeLists.txt:979-980). Device selection requires acceleration_structure + ray_tracing_pipeline + buffer_device_address (vulkan/ChVulkanRTDevice.cpp:81-147; ChVulkanRTUtils.cpp:89-98). env.sh's note of a ~77 s LLVM pipeline compile shows the lavapipe renderer, not Chrono's CPU fallback, is being used.

Tree build runs on the CPU, single-threaded, inside command-buffer execution (lvp_execute.c:4487-4492 → lvp_acceleration_structure.c:264-611). It is linear-time: each triangle's 3 vertices are copied through the index buffer into a 48-byte leaf (343-481), then a balanced binary tree is formed by splitting the primitive list at the index midpoint and computing boxes bottom-up (153-262). There is no spatial sort, so tree quality equals the order Chrono submits triangles in.

Lavapipe 24.2.8 has no refit: lvp_build_acceleration_structure never reads the build mode or source structure, and every build zeroes and rewrites the whole structure (memset at 271). Scratch size is reported as 64 bytes (23); structure size = header + n×(leaf + internal node) (55-59), about 83 MB for ~796.6k triangles.

Ray casting: raygen, closest-hit, miss and any-hit shaders are merged into ONE compute shader and JIT-compiled by LLVM (lvp_ray_tracing_pipeline.c:1025-1107). vkCmdTraceRays becomes a compute grid of 8-ray blocks (1036; lvp_execute.c:641-643, 4552-4583). Traversal is a scalar loop over a two-child tree with a 48-entry stack (lvp_ray_tracing_pipeline.c:359; lvp_nir_ray_tracing.c:385-521), with nearest child first (61-141). There is no batching of rays for SIMD, so cost per ray grows with tree depth (log2 of triangles, ~20 here) and total cost is linear in pixels.

Threading: rays are split across a pool of LP_NUM_THREADS workers (lp_screen.c:1097, 1171-1175; lp_cs_tpool.c:86-107). Default = CPUs in the process affinity mask (u_cpu_detect.c:752-753, 809), capped at 32 (lp_limits.h:69). Work is cut into equal contiguous chunks, one per worker, with no rebalancing (lp_cs_tpool.c:154-155, 57-74), and the calling thread only waits (lp_state_cs.c:1755-1762). LP_NUM_THREADS=0 runs everything serially on the caller (lp_cs_tpool.c:135-144). Only this stage scales with cores.

Scaling expectations (source-based, not measured): tree build and all Chrono-side staging and uploads scale linearly with total triangles and do not use extra cores. Ray casting scales linearly with pixels, roughly with log(triangles), and about inversely with threads up to physical cores, less chunk imbalance (about 30% of rays miss the arena and are cheap). With several processes per node, total threads above the core count degrade ray casting sharply.

Memory: on a software device all Vulkan memory is host RAM. Chrono's upload path still copies each buffer twice (staging, then device-local; ChFilterVulkanRTRender.cpp:2350-2395) and allocates fresh staging, tree, top-level and instance buffers on every rebuild (2366-2369, 2940-2954, 3001-3050). That means page faults and zeroing of hundreds of MB per frame, which is memory-bandwidth-sensitive when runs share a node.

Opaque handling: because the HMMWV chassis has glass materials (hmmwv_chassis.mtl d=0.3/0.2/0.85), the renderer marks the scene transparent and builds the geometry non-opaque (ChFilterVulkanRTRender.cpp:2548-2553, 2920). Depth rays still force opaque (rgen:281-289), so depth cost is unaffected. RGB shadow rays switch to the material-aware loop (rgen:402-445).

Chrono's own CPU fallback (used only if Vulkan device creation fails; ChVulkanRTEngine.cpp:36-47, ChFilterVulkanRTRender.cpp:3605-3831) is not what AMD runs. For reference, it also rebuilds all per-mesh trees whenever the scene version changes (3608-3611, 801-853), spawns std::thread::hardware_concurrency() threads per frame (3807-3831), and copies a string-laden material record on every closer hit (1090).

amd.summary:
I ran every config in the matrix on the AMD cluster using the shared harness. I also ran a second test that splits each frame into its two costs. Every config finished, and the results are synced to /home/harry/NeDM-traverse_mppi/artifacts/traverse/fdm_f104_50h_20260909/render_latency_v1/amd/.

**Why it is slow.** Two separate costs add up to the ~2.6 s frame on a 16-CPU node:

1. **Ray tracing on the CPU (about 70% at 1024x1024).** The software Vulkan driver spends a steady ~27 microseconds of CPU per pixel, so a 1024x1024 frame needs ~28 CPU-seconds. On 16 threads that is 1.9 s.
2. **A full scene rebuild before every frame (~0.8 s on the 16-CPU nodes, ~0.5 s on the 128-core nodes).** This cost does not change with image size. When any body moves at all, Chrono's Vulkan code copies the whole scene again (the 522k-triangle ground plus the 273k-triangle HMMWV), merges it into one triangle list, uploads it and rebuilds the search tree the ray tracer uses. The parked vehicle is enough to trigger it: every static and every moving frame rebuilt.

**How each part behaves:**
- **Pixels:** on one node, the no-rebuild frame at 16 threads went 0.12 → 0.49 → 1.9 → 7.7 s from 256 to 2048. That is exactly 4x per doubling of the image side, while the rebuild stayed constant. Tracing dominates at 1024 and above; the rebuild dominates at 512 and below.
- **Static vs moving:** no difference, because both rebuild every frame.
- **Threads:** tracing scales almost perfectly. At 512 the no-rebuild frame took 7.1 / 3.9 / 2.1 / 1.0 / 0.49 s for 1 / 2 / 4 / 8 / 16 threads, and CPU time stayed flat. The rebuild runs on one thread and does not speed up.
- **Thread cap:** the driver (Mesa 24.2.8) caps its workers at 32. On the 128-core node, 32, 64 and 128 threads all gave 1.43–1.47 s at 1024. That, 1.4 s, is the practical floor for this setup.
- **RGB camera:** at 1024 on 16 threads the frame goes from 2.7 s to 6.6 s. Its tracing costs about twice the depth camera's; the rebuild is shared, not repeated.
- **First frame:** 1–2 s slower than later frames (4.7 vs 2.7 s at 1024 on 16 CPUs), mostly one-time setup of the ray-tracing program in the driver. Scene build itself is only 0.4–0.7 s. Timings assume the shared shader cache is warm; I did not re-test with it empty.

**What the controls showed:**
- **CPU profile:** 92% of CPU time is in the driver's compiled ray-tracing code. On the main thread, the rebuild is about half Chrono copying triangles and half the operating system handing out fresh memory. Building the search tree itself is only ~0.04 s.
- **Vehicle hidden:** tracing was barely cheaper (1.85 vs 1.91 s), so the HMMWV mesh is not what makes rays expensive. With no moving geometry the rebuild disappeared, leaving a ~0.18 s change check.
- **Narrower vector math in the driver (128-bit instead of 256-bit):** no effect.

**Sanity check:** the benchmark's depth frames match the stored campaign frame for the same case in all but 0.01% of pixels (near the vehicle, pose ~1 mm apart). They are identical across every thread count and both node types.

**Queue and cost:** all jobs waited at most a few minutes; the longest run was 24 minutes (the 1-thread task); total use was about 1 node-hour.

findings: Two separate costs make up the frame. (1) Tracing: exactly proportional to pixel count, ~27 microseconds of CPU per pixel (25-26 on the 128-core nodes), so 28 CPU-seconds at 1024x1024. (2) Scene rebuild: fixed ~0.75-0.8 s per frame on the 16-CPU VMs and ~0.5 s on the bare-metal 128-core nodes, whatever the image size.
At 1024 on 16 CPUs the 2.7 s frame is 1.9 s tracing (~70%) plus ~0.8 s rebuild. At 256 it is 0.12 s tracing plus 0.8 s rebuild, so smaller images alone can never get below ~0.8 s.

Static equals moving: every static and moving frame in every config rebuilt the scene (confirmed by the Vulkan scene revision counter). A parked vehicle still changes pose/velocity at the 1e-8 level, which invalidates the scene. Frames where only simulated time advances never rebuilt.

What the rebuild is (from the Chrono source plus the profile): ChVulkanRTScene::SyncFromSystem re-stages every triangle (~795k: 522k ground, 173k chassis, ~100k wheels and tires), each with a material record holding 8 strings. ChVulkanRTGpuRenderer::BuildScene merges them into one world-space list (per-triangle vertex and material copies), uploads it and rebuilds a single search tree over everything. Main-thread cost on the VM: ~0.36 s user + ~0.31 s kernel per frame (the kernel part is page faults from reallocating hundreds of MB). The driver's own tree build is only ~0.04 s.

Tracing scales almost perfectly with threads (CPU-seconds per frame stay constant). At 512 on one node: 7.08 / 3.90 / 2.06 / 1.00 / 0.49 s for 1 / 2 / 4 / 8 / 16 threads; 32 threads on the 16-CPU VM was slightly worse (0.55 s). The rebuild is single-threaded and does not scale.

Mesa 24.2.8 llvmpipe caps worker threads at 32 (LP_MAX_THREADS=32 in the source; confirmed at runtime: 67 threads in the process for LP_NUM_THREADS 32, 64 and 128). On mi2104x, LP 32/64/128 all give 1.43-1.47 s at 1024, the floor for this setup: ~0.5 s rebuild + ~0.94 s tracing.

Profile (perf, user-space): 92% of all CPU samples, and essentially all worker-thread time, are in the driver's compiled ray-tracing shader code. Its function names cannot be resolved, so why each ray costs ~27 microseconds is not broken down further.
Hiding the HMMWV meshes barely changes tracing (1.85 vs 1.91 s at 1024), so the vehicle mesh is not what makes rays expensive. It does remove the rebuild entirely, leaving a ~0.18 s change check.
Setting LP_NATIVE_VECTOR_WIDTH=128 (the driver reported 128 bits) did not change tracing time (1.90 vs 1.91 s).

RGB camera at 1024, 16 threads: 6.6 s vs 2.7 s depth-only. Its tracing costs ~56 CPU-seconds more (about twice the depth camera's; it also traces a shadow ray and shades). The rebuild is shared, not paid twice.

First frame is 1-2 s slower than later frames: at 1024, 4.7 vs 2.7 s on mi2101x at 16 threads and 3.3 vs 2.3 s on mi2104x at 16 threads; at 256, 2.3 vs 0.9 s. The profile puts ~0.6-0.8 s of it on the main thread in the driver (one-time setup of the ray-tracing program). Scene construction is only 0.4-0.7 s. This is with the shared shader cache already warm.
On the Vulkan path everything happens synchronously inside manager.Update(); picking up the frame afterwards costs under 1 ms depth-only (11 ms with RGB).
Same CPU model on both node types (AMD EPYC 7V13, AVX2, llvmpipe with LLVM 19.1.7 at 256-bit width). The bare-metal node is ~5% faster at tracing and ~40% cheaper per rebuild than the VM.

The benchmark frames match the stored campaign depth frame for g216_v2_group_0000 in all but 0.01% of pixels (vehicle edge, pose differs by ~1 mm). They are identical across thread counts and node types, so this measures the same render the campaign uses.
Consistent with, but not proof of, the 4.3-4.6 s seen when four runs share a 16-CPU node: a dedicated node at 8 threads measures 4.58 s (4 threads: 8.4 s).
problems: The split test (render_split_probe.py) got a small backward-compatible change mid-run: a user vs kernel CPU split and a hide-vehicle option. The first two split runs (mi2101x 16 threads at 256, mi2104x 16 threads at 1024) lack the user/kernel split; all timings are unaffected.
The environment capture's `nproc` line shows 1 because OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 affects nproc. The real CPU affinity (0-15 on mi2101x) is recorded on the next line.

perf could only profile user-space code (perf_event_paranoid=2), and the driver library is stripped, so the ray-tracing code shows up as one unnamed block. The kernel share of the rebuild comes from /proc per-thread CPU accounting, not from perf.
The empty-shader-cache case (~77 s compile, per the note in env.sh) was not re-tested; all first-frame numbers assume the shared Mesa cache is warm.
mi2101x tasks ran on three different VMs (k006-004-v3, k006-005-v4, k006-004-v8). The same-node thread sweep and same-node size sweep reproduce the cross-task numbers within ~5%.
Walltime was well under the limits; nothing timed out or failed. The 1-thread run at 1024 was estimated at 29.6 s per frame, under the 60 s rule, so it was run rather than skipped.

optix_local.summary:
I ran every timing test locally on the RTX 5090 with the OptiX build, and nothing else was using the machine. All timing runs are finished, so the other agent can start its build.

**Speed.** A 1024x1024 depth frame takes 7 ms on the 5090, whether the vehicle is parked or driving. That is about 150 frames per second. The same frame takes about 2.6 s on an AMD node, roughly 350 times slower, and 600 times slower when four runs share a node. Adding the colour camera brings it to 18–25 ms per frame. Starting a new process costs 8.5 s once, almost all of it OptiX compiling its shaders. The first frame after that takes 30–60 ms. Over 300 frames in a row the speed stayed steady at about 140 frames per second depth-only and 40–57 with colour. The GPU used about 1.3 GB (1.4 GB with colour), did not grow, and never went above 4% busy.

**Where the time goes after rendering.** Converting the 1024 frame into the planner's 512x512 height grid takes 54–56 ms on this CPU (a Ryzen 7 5800X, 30 repeats). With the render down to 7 ms, that conversion is now about 88% of the sensing time (61 ms in total), or 70–76% with colour. That is 10–16 frames per second, and the conversion is now the bottleneck. About 10 ms of it is averaging colour even when the colour image is all zeros, as it is in the depth-only runner. Another 11 ms goes to recomputing the per-pixel ray directions, which never change.

**Depth correctness.** The fixed OptiX depth matches the AMD frame of the same case almost exactly. The vehicle ended the settle within 0.7 mm and 2.6 mrad of its position there.
- **Raw depth:** on 721,194 terrain pixels, the differences are at floating-point rounding level: median 0.0000076 m, 99th percentile 0.000023 m, maximum 0.000046 m. None exceed 5 cm, and the error does not grow towards the image edge.
- **Valid pixels:** exactly the same in both frames (70.02%, not one pixel different).
- **Old field-of-view bug: gone.** The best-fit image scale between the two frames is 1.0000005, with no shift. The old bug would give a scale of 0.833. As a control, I applied the old bug to the AMD frame: depth then differed by a median of 1.75 m (up to 4.9 m), and ground positions were off by a median of 5 m (up to 7.9 m).
- **After conversion to the height grid:** coverage is 99.998% in both. Heights agree to a median of 0.000006 m, and all but one cell agree to within 0.00003 m (that cell differs by 1 cm). Both match the arena heightmap to a median of 2 mm and a 99th percentile of 14 mm, once the 511/512 scale correction is applied. Without the correction they drift further apart (6 mm median, 77 mm maximum), which confirms the correction is needed.

**Colour lines up with depth.** The edge of the arena falls on exactly the same pixels in the colour and depth images (0 pixels different, in both the local and AMD frames). The vehicle outline overlaps best with no shift. The colour camera does not change the depth at all: the depth from the colour run is identical to the depth-only run.

Once per process, OptiX spends 8.2-8.4 s compiling shaders, so building the scene takes 8.5-8.9 s; after that the first frame takes 30-60 ms.

Local OptiX depth against the AMD lavapipe frame, same case, pixels within 6 m of either vehicle position excluded (721,194 terrain pixels): median difference 7.6e-6 m, 99th percentile 2.3e-5 m, maximum 4.6e-5 m, i.e. rounding-level agreement, with no growth towards the edge.
Valid-pixel fraction is 0.70016 in both frames, with 0 pixels different.

The old field-of-view bug is gone. The best-fit image scale is 1.0000005 in x and y with a shift below 0.00001 px; a scan from 0.80 to 1.20 bottoms out at exactly 1.00. The old bug would give 0.833. Applying the old bug to the AMD frame as a control gives depth errors of 1.75 m median (up to 4.9 m) and ground-position errors of 5.0 m median (up to 7.9 m).

In the height grid, local and AMD heights agree to a median of 5.7e-6 m and a 99th percentile of 2.2e-5 m on 257,516 cells; one cell differs by 1 cm. Coverage is 0.999985 local and 0.999989 AMD, one cell different.

Both frames match the arena heightmap equally well with the 511/512 correction: grid median 2.0 mm, p99 14 mm, maximum 30 mm; per pixel median 0.01 mm, p99 5.6 mm. Without the correction the error is larger (grid median 6 mm, maximum 77 mm), which confirms the correction is needed.

Colour lines up with depth at 1024 in the local colour-plus-depth run. The off-arena (sky) area covers the same 29.98% of pixels in both images with 0 pixels different, so the arena edge falls on the same pixels. The vehicle outline in colour overlaps the depth outline best with no shift (overlap 0.78). The AMD frame gives the same results. The local and AMD colour images have identical sky areas, and the blue roof marker sits within 0.1 px in both.
The colour camera does not affect depth: depth from the colour-plus-depth run is bit-identical to the depth-only run.

Side note: the terrain colour differs between the two machines, brown locally and green-grey on AMD. Local terrain median RGB is (173,147,110) against (185,198,162) on AMD, a mean difference of about 50/255 in green and blue. The local colour matches grass_texture.jpg (162,140,105), so the AMD run probably used the plain fallback colour. Depth is unaffected, but any model that reads colour would see different inputs.
Side note: the 0.8 s settle took 12.2-12.5 s of physics wall time locally (about 31 ms per step), while driving physics ran at about 1.9 ms per step (0.25 s simulated in 0.256 s).
problems: GPU memory was sampled with nvidia-smi from a background thread, which gets no samples while the scene builds (OptiX shader compilation holds the Python lock). So I have no peak memory figure for the build; the numbers cover settling and rendering only. The early 'before build' reading is inconsistent between the two runs (763 MiB vs 173 MiB) because it was taken around when CUDA started up.

The vehicle-outline check is coarse: the colour outline is found by thresholding colour against the surrounding terrain, which misses the darker rear of the vehicle (overlap 0.78 locally, 0.70 on AMD). The arena-edge check is the precise registration test, with an exact match.

I did not separate the 5.9 ms inside manager.Update() at 1024 into GPU ray tracing versus copying the frame back from the GPU. The low GPU load (1-4%) suggests the copy dominates, but I did not measure it.
Only one case was compared (g216_v2_group_0000), and only at 1024 against AMD, the one size stored for it.

vulkan_local.summary:
I built Chrono locally with only the Vulkan ray-tracing renderer, the same setup as the AMD build, and ran the shared test script three ways. Nothing else was using the machine, and every log names the device that was actually used.

**The AMD slowness reproduces here.** I copied the cluster's own software ray tracer (lavapipe, from Mesa 24.2.8) and ran it on this 8-core Ryzen. A 1024 depth frame took 2.45 s (AMD: 2.6 s). Its terrain depth matches the stored AMD frame bit for bit. So the AMD processors are not the problem; the software is.

**The same code on the RTX 5090 is not real time either.** It takes 0.69–0.81 s per frame at every image size from 256 to 2048. OptiX on the same card takes 7 ms. The GPU was mostly idle (6.5% busy on average, under 1 GB of memory).

**Why.** Whenever anything moved since the last frame, this renderer rebuilds its whole scene on the CPU. That is always true while driving, and even with the vehicle parked, because one physics step moves the bodies by micrometres. The rebuild includes the 522,242 terrain triangles that never move:
- copying and checking every triangle: about 0.5 s on one CPU thread;
- merging everything into one list and uploading it: about 0.2 s on one thread;
- rebuilding the ray-tracing search structure from scratch.

When I advanced only the clock and nothing moved, a 1024 frame took 4 ms on the 5090.

**What dominates each case (1024 frame, vehicle moved):**
- **5090:** about 0.7 s of that CPU rebuild; the GPU work is under 0.1 s.
- **Mesa 25.2.8 lavapipe (this machine's own), 16 threads:** 0.5 + 0.2 + about 0.46 s structure rebuild + 0.06 s tracing = 1.2 s.
- **AMD's Mesa 24.2.8 lavapipe:** 0.5 + 0.2 + about 0.1 s structure rebuild + 1.67 s tracing = 2.45 s.

On AMD, CPU ray tracing is the largest single part (about 68%). The roughly 0.8 s rebuild is paid on every device, and it is what keeps even the 5090 from being real time.

**The Mesa version alone doubles the speed.** On this CPU, the newer Mesa 25.2.8 traces 26 times faster and gives 1.12–1.21 s per frame. Its depth still matches AMD to 0.000023 m.

**Depth correctness.** Compared with the AMD frame on 721,194 terrain pixels (6 m around both vehicle positions excluded), the pixels with valid depth were identical in every case:
- 5090: median 0.0000076 m, 99th percentile 0.000023 m, max 0.000038 m.
- Local Mesa 25.2.8: median 0, 99th percentile 0.000015 m, max 0.000023 m.
- AMD's lavapipe on this CPU: exactly 0.

**One deviation you should know about.** Your Chrono source at /home/harry/chrono cannot produce a usable Vulkan-only Python module: without OptiX it has no depth camera. The AMD build only works because its source tree has 7 uncommitted Python-binding files. Rather than edit anything, I built from a separate copy: the exact commit AMD was built from (its sensor code is identical to your fork's), plus those 7 files copied unchanged from AMD. /home/harry/chrono and its build are untouched, and the compiled Vulkan shaders are byte-identical to AMD's.

findings: Reproduced locally: the AMD cluster's own lavapipe (Mesa 24.2.8), copied here and run on this 8-core Ryzen 7 5800X, takes 2.45 s per 1024 depth frame with 16 threads, against 2.6 s on the AMD node. Its terrain depth matches the stored AMD frame bit for bit on all 721,194 terrain pixels. The AMD processors are not the problem; the software is.

The same code on the RTX 5090 (through the NVIDIA Vulkan driver) is not real time either: 0.69-0.81 s per frame at every size from 256 to 2048, and 0.77 s with colour. OptiX on the same card takes 7 ms, about 100 times faster. The GPU averaged 6.5% busy (peak 68%) and used under 1 GB of memory.

Root cause, from code plus tests: whenever any body's position or velocity changed since the last frame, the renderer rebuilds the whole scene on the CPU. That is true every frame while driving, and even with the vehicle parked, because one physics step moves bodies by micrometres. The harness's 'static' and 'moving' results are therefore the same. The rebuild copies and checks every triangle, including the 522,242 terrain triangles that never move (ChVulkanRTScene.cpp, SyncFromSystem). It then merges everything into one world-space list, uploads it and rebuilds a single ray-tracing search structure from scratch (ChFilterVulkanRTRender.cpp, Render -> BuildScene -> BuildAccelerationStructures). When I advanced only the clock and nothing moved, a 1024 frame took 4 ms on the 5090, 63 ms on local lavapipe and 1.67 s on AMD's lavapipe.

Per-frame breakdown, 1024 depth, vehicle moved. RTX 5090: copying and checking the triangles 0.48 s (one CPU thread), merging and uploading about 0.21 s (one thread), GPU rebuild plus tracing plus read-back under 0.1 s; total 0.75-0.81 s. Mesa 25.2.8 lavapipe, 16 threads: 0.49 + about 0.2 + search-structure rebuild about 0.46 s (about 6 CPU-seconds over 16 threads) + tracing 0.063 s = 1.22 s. AMD's Mesa 24.2.8 lavapipe, 16 threads: 0.49 + about 0.2 + rebuild about 0.1 s + tracing 1.67 s (about 25 CPU-seconds) = 2.45 s. On AMD, CPU ray tracing is the largest single part (about 68%). The roughly 0.8 s scene rebuild is paid on every device and is what keeps even the 5090 from being real time.

The Mesa version alone is worth 2x. On this CPU, the newer local lavapipe (Mesa 25.2.8) traces the 1024 frame 26 times faster than AMD's Mesa 24.2.8 (0.063 s vs 1.67 s), for 1.12-1.21 s per frame instead of 2.45 s. Upgrading the cluster's portable lavapipe should roughly halve the AMD render time, but it cannot go much below about 1 s because of the rebuild.

Scaling. With Mesa 25.2.8 the frame time hardly depends on image size (1.16 / 1.18 / 1.21 s at 256 / 512 / 1024) or threads (1.38 / 1.21 / 1.21 s at 4 / 8 / 16), because the fixed rebuild dominates. With AMD's Mesa 24.2.8 both matter (0.91 / 1.24 / 2.45 s by size; 5.39 / 3.17 / 2.45 s at 4 / 8 / 16 threads), because tracing dominates. On this 8-core, 16-thread chip, going from 8 to 16 threads helps only 1.3x.

Sharing the machine. Four runs at once here (16 threads each, 8 physical cores): AMD's lavapipe 7.6-7.8 s per frame each, 3.1x slower than alone; Mesa 25.2.8 3.0-3.7 s. This is the same effect as the 4.3-4.6 s seen on AMD when four runs share a node; this machine has fewer cores, so the slowdown is steeper.

Colour camera. On the 5090 it adds 0.07 s; with Mesa 25.2.8 it adds 0.14 s. With AMD's Mesa 24.2.8 the frame goes from 2.45 s to 6.1 s. Adding colour does not change the depth; the frames are identical.

Start-up. Building the Vulkan scene takes 0.3-0.7 s; there is no 8 s OptiX shader compile. The first 5090 frame takes about 1 s. The first lavapipe frame with an empty Mesa shader cache takes 31 s (Mesa 25.2.8) or 63 s (AMD's Mesa 24.2.8) to compile the ray-tracing pipeline once; with a warm cache it takes 2.4-3.5 s. Peak memory per run was 2.2-2.5 GB (3.8 GB on the cold-cache compile).

Depth correctness against the AMD frame. 721,194 terrain pixels compared; 12,976 pixels within 6 m of either vehicle position excluded; valid-pixel masks identical (70.02%) in every case. Settled vehicle position here differs from AMD by 0.66 mm and 2.6 mrad. Vulkan on 5090: median 0.0000076 m, 99th percentile 0.000023 m, max 0.000038 m, no pixel over 5 cm. Local lavapipe (Mesa 25.2.8): median 0, 99th percentile 0.000015 m, max 0.000023 m; 91% of pixels bit-identical. AMD's lavapipe on this CPU: 0 / 0 / 0, all bit-identical. Vulkan on 5090 vs the OptiX frame: median 0.000015 m, max 0.000061 m.

Planner height grid (after conversion) against AMD. 5090: median 0.0000055 m, 99th percentile 0.000018 m; one cell differs by 1.6 cm and one cell differs in coverage (99.998% vs 99.999%), the same pattern the OptiX check found. Mesa 25.2.8: 99th percentile 0.0000076 m, max 0.0074 m. AMD's lavapipe on this CPU: identical grid. Within each lavapipe version, depth is bit-identical across 4, 8 and 16 threads and when four runs share the machine.

claims.claim: The full scene rebuild runs on every frame in which any body moved at all, even by micrometres. That includes a parked vehicle after a single physics step, so parked and driving frames cost the same. The rebuild is skipped only when nothing but the simulated clock advances. The cause is in the code. Chrono's Vulkan scene fingerprints and compares every body's pose and velocity. It copies every triangle into a new list before checking whether anything changed. On any change it bumps the scene revision, and the renderer then flattens and re-uploads the whole scene and rebuilds one search structure over all ~795k triangles from scratch, with no update-in-place.

claims.claim: On AMD, the CPU time of a rebuild frame is spent mostly in Chrono's code, not the driver. The main thread's time goes to Chrono copying triangles into its staging list and merging them (FillTrianglePrimitive, AddMesh, copies of the per-triangle records, string assignments, memmove). Nearly half of that main-thread CPU time is operating-system (kernel) time: about 0.33 of 0.70 CPU-s per frame on the VM and 0.16 of 0.42 on bare metal. That fits freshly allocating hundreds of MB each frame. Across the whole profiled process, 92% of CPU samples fall in the driver's compiled ray-tracing code.

claims.claim: The HMMWV mesh is not what makes each ray expensive. With the vehicle's visual meshes hidden, the frame with nothing moved took 1.85 s, against 1.98 s for the full scene on the same VM. Hiding the vehicle also stopped all rebuilds, yet about 0.18 s of main-thread CPU per frame remained in the parked and driving cases. The AMD summary calls that a 'change check'. The source investigation predicted exactly this case: hidden vehicle parts keep empty visual models, which still change the fingerprint, so Chrono keeps copying and comparing the 522k terrain triangles without bumping the revision. A 21-body fingerprint walk alone should cost far less than 0.18 s, so the source explanation is the more plausible one, but neither was measured directly. Removing the vehicle bodies from the rendered system entirely should remove this remainder too; that is untested.

About 1.91 s (roughly 70%) is ray tracing done on the CPU by lavapipe from Mesa 24.2.8. This extra cost does not grow with image size, but it varies between nodes: about 0.64 s on another mi2101x node, where tracing is about 76% of a 2.6 s frame. On the 128-core bare-metal node at 16 lavapipe threads the frame takes 2.29 s: 1.82 s tracing plus 0.48 s of per-frame scene work. verdicts.reasoning:
I tried to break the two-part explanation and couldn't. The source code, the stored measurements and the profiler output all agree with it.

What the code does (Chrono sensor source, which the provenance file says matches the AMD build): on each sensor update, ChVulkanRTEngine::UpdateSensors calls ChVulkanRTScene::SyncFromSystem. That function hashes every body's pose and velocity. If the hash changed, it re-copies every visible shape's triangles (FillTrianglePrimitive) and compares the result with the previous copy. If anything differs, it bumps the scene revision. ChVulkanRTGpuRenderer::Render then sees the new revision and calls BuildScene. BuildScene flattens every triangle, including the static terrain, into one world-space list, re-uploads all the buffers, and destroys and rebuilds the single bottom-level and top-level ray-tracing search structures from scratch. Only then does it trace, inside the same Update() call. So "a rebuild of the whole scene before the trace" is literally what the code does. It is triggered by any body movement, which happens on every frame when driving and even when parked, because of tiny settling motions.

Checks against other explanations:
- **Timing split / stale frames:** manager.Update() blocks until the frame is done. The frame take is about 0.7 ms. The frame tap raises an error if a launch is skipped or has not arrived, so an old frame cannot be counted twice.
- **Warm-up:** the first frame is excluded, and the "frozen_after" regime (1.918 s) matches "frozen" (1.914 s).
- **Contention:** the job had the whole 16-CPU node, the harness and the probe ran one after the other in the same job on the same node (k006-005-v4), and the node was idle at start.
- **Rebuild counter:** the scene revision changed 0 of 5 times in frozen and 5 of 5 in static and moving.

Why the frozen frame is really ray tracing: main-thread CPU was 0.01 s and the worker threads used 28.5 s. Its time grows with pixel count (256: 0.12 s, 512: 0.49 s, 1024: 1.91 s, 2048: 7.70 s) and shrinks in step with more lavapipe threads (1 thread: 28.7 s, 4: 7.7 s, 8: 3.8 s, 16: 1.91 s). In the profile, 99.7% of worker time sits in JIT-compiled lavapipe shader code (the "[JIT]" / perf-map entries).

Why the extra part is the rebuild:
- It stays about 0.7–0.85 s at every image size from 256 to 2048 and at every thread count.
- Main-thread CPU is 0.70 s (about 0.37 s user plus 0.33 s kernel).
- The profiler shows that main-thread time in Chrono's staging and flattening code (FillTrianglePrimitive, AddMesh, copying the primitive list, memmove).
- Control run with the vehicle hidden: the revision never changed and the extra cost fell to about 0.17 s. That leftover is the re-copy-and-compare pass that runs even when nothing visible moved.

Every number in the claim matches the files:
- mi2101x: moving 2.696 s, static 2.759 s, frozen 1.914 s, extra 0.816 s, 27.2 µs of CPU per pixel; 1.914 / 2.73 ≈ 70%.
- mi2104x (no hypervisor listed, 128 CPUs): 2.294 s, 1.817 s tracing, 0.485 s rebuild.
- Other mi2101x nodes give frozen 1.85–1.98 s and an extra 0.64–0.80 s, which is consistent.

Minor caveats. None of them changes the claim:
1. The local cross-check is worded wrongly: 1.672 + 0.497 + 1.978 is not 2.45. The 2.45 s moving frame is staging (0.48–0.50 s) plus Update (1.96–1.98 s). The 1.672 s nothing-moved frame is what that frame should be compared with, which gives about 0.78 s of rebuild locally, matching the AMD number.
2. The rebuild is not unconditional: a frame where no body moved skips it. In the navigation loop that never happens.
3. Most of the rebuild is serial CPU work copying and flattening triangles (about half of it kernel time on the virtual-machine node), not lavapipe's search-structure build, which is barely visible in the profile. About 0.1 s of the 0.82 s is not covered by main-thread CPU.
4. The 1.91 s also includes reading the image back, but that costs about 0.01 s.

verdicts.reasoning:
The core of the claim is right for the scene we actually run, where the vehicle is visible. Two parts are too broad: "any body moved at all" and "every AMD probe file". The project's own no-vehicle probe contradicts both.

What checks out:
- **The data.** I re-counted the scene revision numbers in all 23 AMD probe files. In every file with the vehicle visible, frames where only the clock advanced never rebuilt (0/5 or 0/3). Parked frames after one physics step and driving frames rebuilt every time (5/5 or 3/3). The revision goes up by exactly one per frame: 5 to 10 while parked, 10 to 15 while driving, and stays at 15 afterwards.
- **Parked costs the same as driving.** The driving/parked ratio of median frame times is 0.93 to 1.015 across all files.
- **Local runs.** In all four breakdown files (RTX 5090, system Mesa 25.2.8 and the AMD Mesa build), every one-step and every driving frame changed the scene.
- **The code.**
  - ChVulkanRTScene.cpp 564-571: the fingerprint hashes each body's pose and velocity, rounded to 1e-8, so micrometre moves count.
  - 444-449: the per-object comparison checks pose and velocity with a tolerance of 1e-8.
  - 690-692: the only early return is when the fingerprint is unchanged.
  - 793-801: it builds the full new list of every visible triangle (the static 522k-triangle ground mesh included), compares it with the old one, and bumps the revision if anything differs.
  - ChFilterVulkanRTRender.cpp 2029-2033: a new revision triggers a full rebuild. The whole scene is flattened and re-uploaded, the old search structures are destroyed, and one new one is built from scratch (2923-2929, no update flag). The top-level structure is rebuilt too.
- **Source match.** The source I read is identical to the mirror of the commit the AMD build came from (directory diff).
- **Triangle count.** It is about right: ground mesh (512 px) 522,242, plus the vehicle's chassis, 4 rims and 4 tyres at about 274k. That totals about 796.5k.

What needs qualifying:
1. **The no-vehicle file breaks the "every file" claim.** In probe_2101_lp16_1024_novehicle.json the parked and driving regimes show 0/3 rebuilds; the revision stays at 5 throughout. The vehicle really drove there (0.3 s of physics per frame at 4 m/s) with only its meshes hidden. So bodies can move without a rebuild. The rebuild is only triggered when something that is actually drawn moves or changes velocity by more than about 1e-8.
2. **Moving hidden bodies still cost something.** Hiding the vehicle empties its visual model but keeps it attached (ChPart::RemoveVisualizationAssets calls Clear), so its pose still changes the fingerprint. Each such frame still copies and compares every visible triangle, but does not rebuild. On AMD that costs about 0.17 s on the main thread (2.02 s vs 1.85 s) for zero rebuilds. Bodies with no visual model at all do not enter the fingerprint.
3. **The code comment is misleading on AMD.** The claim quotes a comment saying full rebuilds "dominate runtime", which is not true on AMD at 1024 px. With the vehicle visible, rebuilt minus clock-only frames is:

verdicts.reasoning:
The core mechanism holds, both in the code and in the measurements. A few of the broad statements go further than the evidence.

What holds up:
1. The AMD source matches the local source. build_provenance.json says the AMD build came from commit f54254fa9f. `git diff f54254fa9f -- src/chrono_sensor` is empty, and the Vulkan folder matches the AMD source mirror.
2. The cited lines are right:
   - `HashVisualModelState` (558-571) hashes each body's pose and its linear and angular velocity. Values are rounded to 1e-8, so micrometre changes register.
   - `SamePrimitive` (444-449) compares frame and velocities with a 1e-8 tolerance.
   - Lines 690-692 return early only when the fingerprint is identical.
   - Lines 694-790 rebuild the full staged list, triangle by triangle. Lines 797-801 compare it and call `Touch()`, which bumps the revision.
   - `Render` (2029-2033) calls `BuildScene` whenever the revision differs. `BuildScene` clears and re-flattens every triangle into world space and re-uploads all buffers.
   - `BuildAccelerationStructures` destroys the old structures, then builds one bottom-level structure with MODE_BUILD, PREFER_FAST_TRACE and no allow-update flag, plus a one-instance top-level structure. There is no update-in-place.
   - The renderer is shared between sensors, so there is one rebuild per frame, not one per camera.
3. The ~795k triangle figure checks out: terrain 522,242 plus HMMWV OBJ files (chassis 172,563, 4 rims at 12,381, 4 tires at 13,056) makes about 796.6k.
4. The data matches the claim:
   - Every AMD probe shows 0 revision bumps for time-only frames and for time-only frames after driving, and a bump on every one-step and every driving frame.
   - The time-only frames before and after the other regimes rule out warm-up.
   - Frame totals include the take and the revision is read after the take, so async timing and stale frames are not a concern.
   - Parked and driving frames cost the same within noise (for example 2.77 s vs 2.73 s at 1024 px with 16 threads). Main-thread CPU is about 0.7 s on those frames and about 0.01 s on time-only frames.
   - The local breakdown agrees on the 5090, on Mesa 25.2.8 and on the AMD Mesa build.

What needs qualifying:
(a) "Runs on every frame in which any body moved at all" and "skipped only when nothing but the simulated clock advances" are too broad, and the project's own no-vehicle control contradicts them. In probe_2101_lp16_1024_novehicle.json the hidden vehicle physically drove 0.25 s before each frame, yet the revision stayed at 5 on all 3 static and all 3 moving frames. The main thread still spent about 0.18 s per frame (static 0.17-0.18, moving 0.17-0.18) re-copying and comparing the terrain triangles.
   - Why: hiding a vehicle part calls `ChVisualModel::Clear()` (ChPart.cpp:475-478), which leaves an empty visual model behind. So the fingerprint still changes, but the staged list is identical and `Touch()` is never called.
   - The accurate trigger is a change larger than 1e-8 in the pose or velocity of a body with at least one visible shape (or a material or shape change). It is two-stage: the copy cost is paid whenever the cheap fingerprint changes, and the rebuild only when the renderable list differs.
   - In the real runner scene the vehicle is visible, so the practical conclusion stands.
(b) "Even by micrometres" was never measured. No script records how far the parked vehicle moves in one step. The breakdown docstring asserts it. The code tolerance makes it plausible, and a velocity change alone would also trigger a rebuild.
(c) "Copies every triangle before checking whether anything changed" gets the order slightly wrong. A cheap fingerprint check comes first; the full copy happens only when that check says something changed, and the detailed comparison comes after the copy.
(d) The quoted comment that rebuilds "dominate runtime" is a developer remark about the GPU case. It does not describe the AMD cost.
   - At 1024 px on 16 threads, a rebuild adds only about 0.5-0.9 s to a 2.7 s frame (roughly 20-33%). A frame with no rebuild still takes 1.9 s of pure lavapipe ray tracing (1.8 s on the 2104 node).
   - The rebuild dominates only on the 5090 (0.004 s vs about 0.75 s) and at small image sizes (256 px on AMD: 0.12 s vs 1.0 s).
   - The local AMD-Mesa run on this workstation needs 1.67 s for a time-only frame, against 0.065 s with the system Mesa 25.2.8. So the rebuild is not the main reason the AMD frame is slow.
(e) Two small citation errors:
   - The flag in the bd_*.json files is `scene_rebuilt_each_frame`. `scene_rebuilt_every_frame` only appears in summary_table.json.
   - The local one_step flag comes from an explicit `SyncFromSystem` call made before `manager.Update()`, not from `Update` itself. It is still a valid test of the trigger.
   - On AMD, "rebuilt" means the revision changed. That `BuildScene` actually ran is inferred from the code and supported by the 0.5-0.9 s timing gap.

verdicts.corrected_claim:
In the runner scene the vehicle is visible, and the full Vulkan scene rebuild then runs on every frame after even one physics step. That includes a parked vehicle, so parked and driving frames cost the same. Only time-only frames skip it.

The precise trigger is two-stage. First, Chrono computes a cheap fingerprint of each body's pose and velocity (bodies with no visual model contribute only an identity pointer). If that fingerprint changed, it re-copies every triangle and compares the copy with the previous one. Only if the renderable list actually differs does it bump the revision. A difference here means a body with a visible shape moved or changed velocity by more than 1e-8. When the revision is bumped, the renderer re-flattens and re-uploads all ~796k triangles and rebuilds one bottom-level search structure from scratch, with no update-in-place.

Bodies with no visible shapes do not trigger a rebuild, but can still cost the copy. With the vehicle hidden, driving caused no rebuild but still cost about 0.18 s per frame of copying.

On AMD at 1024 px with 16 threads, the rebuild adds about 0.5-0.9 s to a roughly 2.7 s frame. The remaining ~1.9 s is lavapipe ray tracing, so the rebuild is a real but minority cost there. The micrometre scale of the parked vehicle's movement was not measured.

verdicts.reasoning:
I recomputed every number from the raw files, and they all match. The main point holds. On the RTX 5090, a Vulkan frame takes about 0.7 s whenever anything in the scene has moved, and about 4-9 ms when nothing has. OptiX on the same card takes 0.5-7 ms at sizes 256-1024, so the slowness belongs to the Vulkan code path. Four details in the claim need correcting or softening.

What checks out:
- **Per-size medians:** recomputed from the 30 raw frames per size and regime in vk5090_depth.json. Sizes 256/512/1024/2048 give 0.740/0.812/0.694/0.694 s when the vehicle is parked (one physics step between frames) and 0.745/0.743/0.705/0.737 s when it is driving. These match summary_table.json exactly.
- **GPU and driver:** the log names the NVIDIA driver file 12 times and prints "Vulkan RT device: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090" once per size, so there was no quiet fallback to software rendering. nvidia-smi shows the card otherwise idle (173 MiB baseline) and only 6.5% average use, which fits a GPU that is mostly waiting.
- **The frames are real:** the harness refuses to accept a frame unless the launch counter goes up by exactly one, so the fast "nothing moved" frames were genuinely rendered.
- **The Chrono source agrees with the story.** Any change in a body's position or velocity changes a cheap scene fingerprint. That makes Chrono re-copy every triangle in the scene, including all 522,242 terrain triangles, work out their normals, tangents and texture coordinates again, and compare the whole list with the previous frame. The renderer then merges everything into one world-space list, uploads it, and rebuilds the ray-tracing acceleration structure from scratch.
- **Staging is single-threaded:** the staging step's CPU time on the main thread equals its wall time (0.485 vs 0.485 s), with other threads near zero.

What needs qualifying:
1. **The 4 ms "nothing moved" figure is the lower of two measurements.** The same run measured nothing-moved frames twice. The first batch had a median of 4.0 ms. The second batch, after the driving frames, had a median of 8.8 ms (three of five frames at 8.8-9.5 ms). Waiting for and copying the frame adds another 0.3 ms. "4-9 ms" is the honest figure.
2. **The split between CPU and GPU is misleading.** The 0.27-0.33 s second stage is not mostly GPU time. Main-thread CPU was 0.205-0.214 s of it in every frame. Adding staging, main-thread CPU is about 0.69 s of a 0.74-0.81 s rebuilt frame (85-94%). Only about 0.06-0.12 s is spent outside the main thread (structure build, trace and readback). Some of that 0.21 s may be the NVIDIA driver working or busy-waiting in the calling thread, so CPU time alone cannot fully separate the two. Still, "0.48 s on one CPU thread plus 0.27-0.33 s of merge/upload/GPU build/trace" understates how much of the frame is single-thread CPU work.
3. **The 1024 breakdown comes from a separate, small run.** It used 5 frames per regime, not the benchmark's 30-frame run. Its per-frame totals (median 0.740 s parked, 0.810 s driving) are 7-15% above the benchmark's 1024 medians (0.694 / 0.705 s). That is close, but the parts do not add up exactly to the headline number, and no breakdown exists for the other sizes.
4. **"Real time" is loose, and the size range describes medians.** "0.69-0.81 s at every size" describes medians only; single frames ranged from 0.60 to 0.84 s. The claim never defines "real time". The result is about 1.2-1.4 frames per second. That is far below any camera frame rate, but for a loop that renders one frame per planning decision at 1-2 Hz it is borderline rather than clearly ruled out.

verdicts.reasoning:
The main point holds, both in the source code and in the measurements. On the RTX 5090, a Vulkan frame is slow because the whole scene is rebuilt every time anything moves. What the renderer does when nothing moves costs almost nothing. Details of the wording need correcting.

What holds:
- **The numbers match.** summary_table.json matches vk5090_depth.json. Frame medians are 0.740/0.812/0.694/0.694 s (parked) and 0.745/0.743/0.705/0.737 s (moving) at sizes 256/512/1024/2048, 30 frames each. The first frame is excluded.
- **The NVIDIA driver was really used.** The log shows the loader opening libGLX_nvidia.so.0 and "Vulkan RT device: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090". GPU memory sat at 173 MiB before the run, so nothing else was using the card. The build is Release -O3.
- **No async or stale-frame effect.** The render call records, submits and waits for the GPU to finish, then copies the result to host memory, all inside manager.Update(). take_s is only 0.1–2 ms. The frame reader also demands exactly one new launch per read.
- **The rebuild is the cause.** Chrono computes a cheap hash of body poses and velocities. If it is unchanged, nothing is rebuilt and the frame is only a trace plus a copy back. If any body moved, Chrono re-extracts every triangle and bumps a revision counter. The renderer then flattens all triangles into one world-space list, re-uploads it, and rebuilds the single bottom-level and top-level GPU acceleration structures from scratch. The breakdown test changes only whether bodies moved. It confirms the rebuild happened on every step or drive frame and never on the time-only frames.
- **The explicit staging call does not double-count.** After it, the hash inside Update() matches and returns early. This is a Vulkan-only build, so there is no OptiX light-mirroring step either.
- **"One CPU thread" holds.** Staging used 0.485 s of main-thread CPU for 0.485 s of wall time, and other threads used about 0.001 s.

What needs correcting:
1. **The time is not spent "checking" triangles.** Body 0 is the vehicle chassis (a 172,563-triangle mesh). I confirmed this by building the same scene locally without a camera. The comparison looks at pose and velocity before any triangles, and the chassis changes after every physics step. So the comparison stops at the first shape and no triangle is ever compared. The 0.48 s is re-extracting all 796,553 triangles into a new list and freeing the old one. That includes 522,242 unchanged terrain triangles. Each triangle gets its normals and tangent recomputed and a full copy of its material, which holds 8 strings. There are signs that memory churn is a large part of this: 6.4 s of kernel time and 2.5 million minor page faults in the 23 s breakdown run. That is suggestive, not proven.
2. **The remaining 0.27–0.33 s is mostly CPU work too.** It includes about 0.21 s of main-thread CPU, so at most about 0.06–0.12 s is spent waiting on the GPU. So roughly 0.69 of the ~0.75 s is on the one Python/Chrono thread. There is a caveat: the NVIDIA driver may busy-wait while the GPU works. The no-motion frames used 3.5 ms of CPU out of 4 ms, so this split is uncertain.
3. **"4 ms" is the best batch.** The second no-motion batch had a median of 8.8 ms, so 4–9 ms is more accurate. It was measured only at 1024.
4. **The 0.69–0.81 s range is medians.** Single frames ranged from 0.60 to 0.84 s.
5. **"Real time" is never defined.** Whether 0.7 s per frame fails depends on the target rate, e.g. 1–2 planning decisions per second.

None of these reverse the claim. The cited numbers are mostly right, but the description of where the time goes needs correcting.
