verdicts.reasoning:
Every number in the claim matches when recomputed from the raw per-frame files. None were cherry-picked. The problem is the framing. "Software, not processors" is only half right, and two parts are left out.

What checks out:
- **Per-frame times recomputed from the raw lists:**
  - AMD's lavapipe on the local machine: 2.450 s static, 2.460 s moving.
  - Local Mesa 25.2.8: 1.213 s static, 1.122 s moving.
  - The AMD node (k006-005-v4, 16 threads): 2.759 s static, 2.696 s moving.
- **The "nothing moved" frame:** each is the median of 6 frames. AMD's lavapipe gives 1.6725 s and local Mesa gives 0.0632 s, a ratio of 26.5x. In both runs the scene revision did not change, and the worker CPU matches a trace-only frame (24.8 s vs 0.71 s of CPU).
- **Pixel identity:** I compared the npz files directly. The copied AMD lavapipe's frame (and its 4- and 8-thread, four-at-once and colour-plus-depth runs) differs from the stored AMD frame at only 1,202 pixels, all in a 54x35 pixel box at the vehicle. Every other pixel is bit-identical. Local Mesa 25.2.8 differs at 66,130 pixels, by at most about 2e-5 m away from the vehicle.
- **Versions:** the library strings say "Mesa 24.2.8" and "Mesa 25.2.8-0ubuntu0.24.04.2"; dpkg reports libllvm20 20.1.2. The device lines in the logs are as cited.
- **Source:** Mesa 24.2.8's tree build (lvp_acceleration_structure.c, split at line 163) writes the triangles in their original order and splits at the index midpoint. There is no sorting.
- **Run conditions:** the local runs were sequential.

What needs qualifying:
1. **The processor comparison flatters the AMD node.** Both chips are the same generation (Zen 3): the node gives the job 16 cores of an EPYC 7V13 in a VM, while the local 5800X has 8 real cores with 16 threads. At equal thread counts the same software is clearly slower per thread on the node:
   - 8 threads: 4.58 s vs 3.17 s (1.44x).
   - 4 threads: 8.43 s vs 5.39 s (1.56x, on another node).
   - The near-tie at 16 threads (2.70 vs 2.45 s) is partly because the local machine's extra threads are not full cores.
   - Core count also matters a lot on the cluster: a 128-core mi2104x node with the same old Mesa gives 2.29-2.33 s at 16 threads but 1.43-1.47 s at 32 threads or more.
2. **The 26x only applies to tracing.** Per frame, the newer Mesa is 2x faster at 1024. At 512 they are about equal (1.18 vs 1.24 s), and at 256 the newer one is slower (1.16 vs 0.91 s). The reason is that Chrono rebuilds the whole scene every frame:
   - Chrono's main-thread scene copy takes about 0.49 s.
   - Mesa 25.2.8's tree rebuild takes about 0.66 s and 5.7 CPU-seconds, about twice Mesa 24.2.8's roughly 0.31 s.
   - The trace saves 1.61 s, but per frame only about 1.25 s is saved.
3. **Much of what is left is Chrono's Vulkan code, not the CPU renderer.** The same Vulkan-RT path on the RTX 5090 still takes 0.69-0.81 s per frame (0.48 s scene copy plus 0.27-0.33 s update), while OptiX takes under a millisecond. Upgrading Mesa alone cannot make this real time.
4. **The cause is confounded, and the midpoint split is not the only candidate.** The two packages also differ in LLVM version (19.1.7 vs 20.1.2) and build. A quick strings check of the 25.2.8 library shows tree-building code the 24.2.8 library lacks: lbvh_build_internal, lbvh_key, encoded_sah, vk_bvh_geometry_data, and an 8-wide bvh8 intersection routine. That points to a sorted, multi-threaded tree builder, which fits the higher rebuild CPU. It suggests, but does not show, that tree quality is the reason, and tree width, traversal code or LLVM could contribute. Calling the reason untested is fair.

Minor:
- The breakdown used 3+3 frames and the harness 5 frames per regime. The spread is tight, so this does not change anything.
- I could not check the copied library's md5 against the cluster, but the bit-identical frame is strong evidence it is the same build.

verdicts.reasoning:
The measurements hold up. The one cause the claim floats does not.

What checks out:
- **The numbers.** The per-frame figures match the stored results: the cluster's lavapipe (Mesa 24.2.8) on the local CPU takes 2.450 s for a frame after a small step and 2.460 s while driving. Local Mesa 25.2.8 takes 1.213 s and 1.122 s. With nothing moved, the frames take 1.672 s and 0.0632 s, a 26.4x gap. In CPU time the gap is bigger, about 34x: 24.7 vs 0.72 CPU-seconds across the worker threads.
- **The frames are real, fresh and not affected by other runs.** The harness's frame grabber raises an error unless each frame is a new render. Rendering waits for the software renderer to finish, so the grab afterwards takes only 0.4 ms. Warm-up frames are excluded. The run log shows every benchmark ran one at a time.
- **"Nothing moved" really means trace plus readback only.** In Chrono's Vulkan renderer (ChFilterVulkanRTRender.cpp), the scene is only rebuilt when its revision number changes. It did not change in that regime, and the main thread used about 0 CPU.
- **Terrain depth is bit-identical.** All 721,194 terrain pixels match with a maximum difference of 0. The test can tell builds apart: Mesa 25.2.8 matches on only 91% of those pixels. Pixels within 6 m of the vehicle are excluded, and the vehicle pose differs by 0.7 mm.
- **The two CPUs are comparable.** The local machine is a Ryzen 7 5800X (8 cores, 16 threads). The cluster node is a virtual machine with 16 cores of an EPYC 7V13, the same chip generation. On the cluster, 92% of the time is in the renderer's generated tracing code.
- **The source description is accurate.** Lines 153-179 of the 24.2.8 builder split the triangle list at its index midpoint, in the order the triangles were submitted, with no sorting. The downloaded 25.2.8 source instead uses Mesa's shared tree builder with a radix sort.

What needs qualifying:
1. **The named cause is unlikely for this scene.** Chrono writes the terrain triangles row by row (RigidTerrain.cpp) and keeps that order when it flattens the scene. So splitting at the index midpoint already gives a tidy, spatially sorted tree. I rebuilt 24.2.8's tree and traversal in a small C program on the real g216 terrain, with the same camera (47 deg, 110 m). It needs about 31-35 tree steps and 1.4 triangle tests per ray. With about 274k triangles of HMMWV meshes added, it needs 36-40. A spatially sorted tree does worse (75-95 steps). A shuffled list needs about 120,000, which shows the test would catch a bad tree. My vehicle placement was only approximate and I left out the small scene objects. Even so, tree shape cannot produce a 34x gap. The cost per tree step differs by roughly 35-70x instead, about 0.6 µs in 24.2.8 against 8-17 ns in 25.2.8.
2. **The midpoint split is not the only difference.** The 24.2.8 source has a nearest-child-first sort that does nothing (it writes the children back in the same order); 25.2.8 fixes it. My re-implementation says that is worth only about 10%. 25.2.8 also pre-loads each tree step's data (the claim does not mention this), and it ships with LLVM 20.1.2 instead of 19.1.7. Both were installed as packages, not debug builds. None of these was tested on its own, so the cause is still unknown.
3. **"Software" has two layers.** Even on 25.2.8, the trace is only about 5% of the 1.2 s frame. About 0.5 s is Chrono re-copying the whole scene on one thread, and about 0.66 s is rebuilding the tree, because the vehicle moves slightly every step. The RTX 5090 through Vulkan still takes 0.69 s. Updating Mesa alone halves the time but does not reach real time.
4. **Minor: which cluster number.** On the MI2101X partition, 2.70 s is the moving-regime figure; the static figure is 2.76 s. The MI2104X partition gave 2.29 s at 16 threads, faster than the local 2.45 s, which supports the claim.

1. **Real time only for rendering.** In the same 300-frame drive, the physics alone took 47.5 ms per 50 ms of simulated time (0.95 s of wall time per simulated second). At the planner's 1-2 decisions per second, rendering is negligible and the loop overall runs just barely faster than real time.

verdicts.reasoning:
The headline numbers are real and the timing method holds up against the Chrono source. But a few parts of the claim say more than the evidence shows.

What holds:
1. Every cited number matches the files. Depth-only while driving: median 6.93 ms, p99 8.27 ms, 300 frames, 144.3 frames/s. Depth back-to-back: 7.29 ms. With colour: 17.55 ms while driving and 25.20 ms back-to-back. Process GPU memory: 1278 MiB. In the earlier 30-frame bench, 1024 depth took 6.79 ms parked and 7.34 ms moving.
2. The timing captures a finished frame, not just a queued request. With lag 0 and collection window 0 (set in scene.py), ChOptixEngine::UpdateSensors does not return until that sensor's render thread is done. The render thread runs the OptiX render, the depth-to-RGBA8 step and the pinned-memory GPU-to-host copy, then calls cudaStreamSynchronize before it marks itself done. So manager.Update() blocks until the frame is on the host. The take step is only unwrapping plus the numpy copy and flip (about 1.3 ms).
3. The frames are not stale. The render filter stamps LaunchedCount at render time and the access filter carries it along with the data. The frame reader in scene.py raises an error unless each frame's launch count is exactly the previous one plus one.
4. The slow first frame (47 ms, the one that builds the scene) is in the sample but barely moves the median.
5. The two backends draw the same picture. OptiX and the AMD frame differ by at most 4.6e-5 m on terrain, the valid-pixel masks agree on every pixel, and the best-fit scale is 1.000. So the speed-up compares identical output.

What needs qualifying:
(a) "Real time" is true for the render only. In the same run, one render every 50 ms of simulated time, the whole loop ran at 0.89x real time with depth (16.77 s of wall time for 15 s simulated) and 0.76x with colour. Physics took about 47.5 ms per 50 ms and is the real limit. The sustained test also only ran at 20 Hz and about 190 Hz. The real planner renders at 1–2.4 Hz with the GPU idle in between, and that pattern was never tested.
(b) "About 390x" is 2.696 s divided by 6.93 ms, which mixes two different test scripts. Using the same script on both machines gives 367x while moving and 406x while parked. The AMD figure is also a median of only about 8 frames.
(c) The colour numbers are not a stable property of how often you render. Within the colour run, the driving phase fell from about 17.8 ms to about 15.3 ms, and the back-to-back phase climbed from about 15.0 ms (first 10 frames) to about 25 ms (last 10). Almost all of the extra back-to-back time is in the take step (15.4 ms vs 7.5 ms). The Update step, which contains the GPU render, was actually slightly faster (9.8 ms vs 10.1 ms). The source explains why the take step can vary. The access filter allocates a new pinned host buffer every frame, and the previous frame's buffer is released inside the take step. verdicts.reasoning:
The headline numbers check out, and the measurements behind them hold up. The claim needs qualifying in three places: why the thread counts stop helping, what "no rebuild" really leaves behind, and the "only with both changes" conclusion.

What is confirmed:
- **AMD, 128-core node (mi2104x), whole node in one job:** each 1024 depth frame took 1.435 s at 32 threads, 1.434 s at 64 and 1.427 s at 128. Frames where nothing moved took 0.937, 0.935 and 0.939 s. No 1024 run on AMD did better.
- **Mesa version on AMD:** every AMD probe file and log points at the toolchain lavapipe, which reports "Mesa 24.2.8 / LLVM 19.1.7". Nothing on AMD ever ran Mesa 25.2.8.
- **Local Mesa 25.2.8:** a frame with nothing moved took 0.063 s, with 16 threads on the Ryzen 7 5800X, which has 8 cores.
- **No render-only-system run exists anywhere** under render_latency_v1.

The measurement worries do not apply:
- **Timing is not async:** the frame render happens inside manager.Update(), and the frame take afterwards costs 0.4 ms.
- **The no-rebuild frames are not stale:** each one used about 27 CPU-seconds of lavapipe worker time, and the scene revision counter shows 0 rebuilds for them versus 5 of 5 for moving frames.
- **No warm-up effect:** the nothing-moved frames measured again after the moving ones took 0.96 s, the same as the first set.
- **The mechanism matches the source:** in ChVulkanRTScene.cpp, SyncFromSystem hashes every body's pose and velocity. If the hash changes, it re-walks the shapes and, when they differ, calls Touch(). Render() then runs BuildScene, which flattens everything into one list, re-uploads it and rebuilds one acceleration structure over all triangles, the 522k-triangle terrain included. Even the parked one-physics-step frames rebuild every time.
- **Mesa is the right thing to blame:** the same Ryzen with AMD's Mesa 24.2.8 build needs 1.67 s for a nothing-moved frame. That is 23.6 CPU-microseconds per pixel, against 25.8 on AMD and 0.68 with Mesa 25.2.8. So the gap comes from the Mesa build, not the AMD CPU. In Mesa 24.2.8, lavapipe's acceleration-structure builder splits the triangle list in half by position in the list, with no spatial sort (lvp_acceleration_structure.c:163). That is a plausible cause, though LLVM 19 versus 20 was not ruled out.

Qualifications:
1. **"32 or more threads" is really "32 threads".** Mesa 24.2.8 has a hard cap: LP_MAX_THREADS is 32 (lp_limits.h:69) and lp_screen.c:1175 clamps the thread count to it. All three runs had 67 threads in the process, against 35 at 16 threads. So the flat result is a driver limit, not a sign that more cores stop helping; the 128-core node never used more than 32 render threads.
2. **Removing the rebuild does not remove all per-frame scene work.** The hidden-vehicle probe (probe_2101_lp16_1024_novehicle, 16 threads) shows it:
   - Moving frames did not rebuild (0 rebuilds), yet took 2.05 s against 1.85 s for nothing-moved frames.
   - The extra was about 0.18 s of main-thread CPU for re-walking and comparing the scene.
   - This happens because the hash includes body poses even when those bodies are invisible.

   So the 0.94 s and 0.063 s figures are only reachable if nothing in the rendered Chrono system moves. That means a render-only system with static terrain and no vehicle in the picture. Hiding the vehicle in the driving system would cost roughly 0.2 s more per frame, and a render-only system with a moving vehicle stand-in would rebuild the whole thing every frame again. The claim treats the frozen frames as the no-rebuild cost without saying this.
3. **"No driving run without the rebuild was tested" overlooks a partial test.** The hidden-vehicle probe drives 0.25 s at 4 m/s between frames without rebuilding. It is only 5 frames on the 16-core partition, not a navigation run, but it is closer than the frozen frames.
4. **"Plausible only with both changes" is overstated.** "Real time" is never given a number. Other untested options exist:
   - Lower resolution without the rebuild already reaches 0.12–0.16 s at 256 and 0.49 s at 512 on AMD's current Mesa with 16 threads.
   - Chrono's own CPU fallback renderer (the path taken when no Vulkan device is found) was never measured on AMD.
5. **Citation slip.** The 0.0632 figure is `nothing_moved_frame_s` in vulkan_local/summary_table.json. bd_lvp16_1024.json has no nothing_moved key; its two nothing-moved medians are 0.0646 and 0.0623 s.

The quoted floors ("about 1.4 s" and "cannot go much below about 1 s") are not in any file, so they could not be checked directly. The numbers are consistent with them: the fastest AMD frame with the rebuild is 1.43 s, and the local Mesa 25.2.8 frames that still include the rebuild are 1.12–1.21 s.

The thread counts recorded inside each process grow with the thread setting (2+t unnamed worker threads plus t llvmpipe threads). The perf profile shows the tracing work in llvmpipe's compiled shader code, so this really is lavapipe. It is not Chrono's own CPU fallback renderer.
3. The explanation matches the code. `manager.Update()` calls `UpdateSensors` and the render filter's `Apply()` synchronously. `ChVulkanRTGpuRenderer::Render` rebuilds only when the scene revision changes. The rebuild (`BuildScene`) loops over all the triangles on the calling thread (`AddMesh`), uploads the buffers, then builds the acceleration structure and waits for it to finish. The frame wait-and-copy step took only ~0.2-0.8 ms, so nothing was left running in the background after `Update()` returned. The recorded revision numbers show frozen frames never rebuilt and static/moving frames always did.
4. The rebuild really is serial. Every rebuilding frame used about 0.6-0.8 s of main-thread CPU at every thread count; frozen frames used about 0. The main point holds up. On the 128-core node, asking lavapipe for 32, 64 or 128 threads gives the same frame time. Going from 16 to 32 threads does help: 2.33 s down to 1.47 s, and the pure ray-tracing frame roughly halves, 1.82 s to 0.94 s. Three details in the claim or its evidence are wrong or incomplete.

What I confirmed:
1. The Mesa code: `lp_limits.h` has `#define LP_MAX_THREADS 32` on line 69, not 68. `lp_screen.c` lines 1171-1175 read `LP_NUM_THREADS` and cap it at 32. Both llvmpipe thread pools are built from that capped number: the drawing pool (line 1091) and the compute pool (line 1097). In lavapipe, ray tracing is sent to the compute pool.
2. The cluster really ran Mesa 24.2.8. The job script read the version string out of the lavapipe library it actually loaded, and the device reports LLVM 19.1.7 and Vulkan API 1.3.289. All four runs were on the same node (k005-002), one after another, with CPU affinity 0-127.
3. I recomputed the timings from the per-run result files and they match the summary. Median of 5 frames at 32/64/128 threads: static 1.470/1.471/1.468 s, moving 1.435/1.434/1.427 s. At 16 threads: 2.331 and 2.294 s. The separate probe runs agree: frozen 0.937/0.935/0.939 s, static 1.497/1.492/1.481 s, moving 1.455/1.444/1.436 s. The quoted "1.43-1.47 s" matches the benchmark runs. The probe's static medians (1.48-1.50 s) fall just outside it, but every measurement shows the three settings within about 1-2%, with overlapping min/max ranges. Nothing was cherry-picked.
4. CPU time per frame is flat at about 27 CPU-seconds whatever the thread count. Frozen frames at 32 or more threads average about 29 busy cores, so the 32-thread limit is the binding one. The perf profile of the 64-thread run saw only 33-34 active threads (main thread plus at most 32 workers).

Qualifications:
(a) "Never more than 32 worker threads" is only true per pool. llvmpipe keeps two pools, each capped at 32, so at 32 or more requested threads the process holds 64 worker threads (67 in total). The cited census entry `llvmpipe-N: 32` counts the drawing pool, and those threads do no work in this job: all worker CPU time sits on threads listed under the name `python`. The ray tracing runs in the compute pool, whose threads don't rename themselves and so show up as `python` threads. That count went from 18 to 34 and stayed at 34 for 64 and 128. So the conclusion is right, but the census entry cited as proof counts the wrong pool.
(b) "Extra cores beyond 32 do nothing" is true for one run's frame time only. The spare cores can still run several independent runs side by side.
(c) About 0.5 s of the roughly 1.45 s frame is the per-frame scene rebuild. Mostly one thread does it: the main thread uses about 0.42 CPU-seconds per moving frame. More cores would not speed that part up even without the 32 cap.
(d) The 32 is a fixed number compiled into Mesa. A Mesa built with a larger limit could change this, which is what "current software stack" should be taken to mean.
(e) Each thread count was run once, with 5 frames each.

verdicts.reasoning:
The main point holds. Only the evidence cited for it and how broadly it is worded need fixing.

What the code does: in the extracted Mesa source, lp_limits.h sets LP_MAX_THREADS to 32. That is line 69, not 68, a trivial slip. lp_screen.c lines 1171-1175 set num_threads to the lower of LP_NUM_THREADS (or the core count) and 32. That one value sizes both of llvmpipe's thread pools: the rasterizer pool at line 1091 and the compute pool at line 1097. In lavapipe, trace-rays commands (handle_trace_rays in lvp_execute.c) call launch_grid, which queues the work on the compute pool (lp_state_cs.c). The AMD node's env dump confirms it runs Mesa 24.2.8 with a 256-bit LLVM 19.1.7 llvmpipe. So the 32-thread cap is real and it does apply to the ray-tracing render.

What needs correcting:
1. The cited count of 32 "llvmpipe-N" threads is the wrong pool. Those are the rasterizer threads, and they do no work for this render. Per-thread CPU in every probe goes only to unnamed threads, which the census labels "python"; threads with zero CPU are dropped from that breakdown. The pool that does the ray tracing is the unnamed compute pool: 18 "python" threads at 16 requested, 34 at 32/64/128. That is 32 compute workers plus the main thread and one other. The same cap applies to it, so the conclusion stands. perf agrees: at 64 requested, only 33-34 threads show samples in any stage.
2. The timings are right, but part of each frame is serial. On the one 128-core node (k005-002), the benchmark medians at 32/64/128 are 1.470/1.471/1.468 s (static) and 1.435/1.434/1.427 s (moving). The probe measured 1.48-1.50 s for the same settings. A frame where nothing moves costs about 0.94 s at all three settings. The extra ~0.5 s in normal frames is a scene rebuild (BVH) on the main thread, and no thread setting touches it. Worker CPU is about 27 s per frame at every setting, so roughly 29 cores are busy at 32 threads. Going from 16 to 32 threads almost halves the trace time (1.82 to 0.94 s). The cap is therefore what limits speed, not a lack of parallel work.
3. "Extra cores beyond 32 do nothing" is only true for the speed of a single render process. Spare cores can still run more renders side by side. The cap is also a compile-time constant in the user-built Mesa, so "current stack" should mean this particular Mesa build.

Other explanations don't fit. Every process could use all 128 cores, and the thread counts match the code's cap exactly. The time to fetch the frame is under 1 ms, so waiting for a late frame is not hiding cost. Each setting ran once, on the same node, and the results differ by less than 1%.

Every number the claim cites is in the files. But the opening sentence is wrong as written, and the explanation for the kernel time points at the wrong code.

What holds up:
- The per-regime CPU breakdown file (perf/perf_2101_lp16_1024_split.txt), '1024/moving' block: the main thread used 1.05 s over 3 frames (wall 8.28 s). 0.83 s of that was in libChrono_sensor.so. The whole-process report shows 92.04% of samples in '[JIT] tid 166649' and 6.30% in libChrono_core.so.
- Kernel time, per frame (medians over 5 frames): main_sys 0.33 of 0.70 CPU-s in probe_2101_lp16_1024.json (a KVM virtual machine). It is 0.16 of 0.42 in probe_2104_lp32_1024.json (bare metal, no hypervisor flag in lscpu). The profile of the same node under perf gives about 0.35-0.37 s of user time per frame, which matches.
- The Chrono source matches the user-space story:
  - ChVulkanRTScene::SyncFromSystem builds a brand-new list of primitives every time the scene's signature changes.
  - FillTrianglePrimitive stores each triangle as a record of about 0.5 KB. Each record carries a full copy of the material, including 8 std::string fields; that is where the string assignments come from.
  - ChFrame declares its own copy constructor and a virtual destructor. So the primitive's implicit move is not noexcept, and growing the vector deep-copies whole triangle lists; that is where the primitive copies come from.
  - BuildScene/AddMesh then flattens everything into one world-space list.
  - The engine runs all of this synchronously inside manager.Update() on the calling thread. update_s holds the whole frame (take_s is about 0.001 s), so frames arriving late or out of order cannot explain the numbers.

What needs qualifying:
1. The first sentence ('the CPU time of a rebuild frame is spent mostly in Chrono's code, not the driver') is false for the frame as a whole. In the same rebuild frames, the driver's worker threads burn about 28.4-29.2 CPU-s against the main thread's 0.70. That is about 97% of the frame's CPU, all in the driver's compiled code, and the same amount is spent in frozen frames that do no rebuild. It is only true of what a rebuild adds on top of a frozen frame, and only for the user-space half of that.
2. The kernel half is not shown to be Chrono's own allocations, and the saved results argue against that reading. perf recorded user space only (cpu-clock:u, paranoid=2), so nobody knows which code paid the 0.33 s, and page faults were never counted. The no-vehicle probe (probe_2101_lp16_1024_novehicle.json, node k006-004-v8) is the check:
   - The vehicle still moves, so Chrono re-stages the 522k-triangle terrain every frame (0.14 s user), but nothing changes and no rebuild happens (rebuilt=False).
   - Its kernel time is only 0.03-0.04 s.
   - With rebuilds on the same node (probe_2101_lp16_1024_vw128.json), kernel time is 0.24-0.33 s.
   So roughly 85-90% of the kernel time comes with the rebuild-and-upload step, not with Chrono's own triangle list. That step makes the driver allocate fresh memory every frame:
   - UploadVector creates a new host-visible staging buffer for every upload (about 290 MB for vertices, materials, indices and triangle ids at 795k triangles).
   - BuildAccelerationStructures creates a new acceleration-structure buffer and scratch buffer each time.
   - Chrono's memcpy then touches the new staging memory for the first time.
   Lavapipe's allocator backs memory with a memfd ('allocation fd' / memfd_create). I confirmed those strings in local Mesa 25.2.8; the cluster's 24.2.8 was not checked. Memory like that is faulted in 4 KB pages, which would explain the high kernel cost, and why it is worse on the VM.
   'Fits freshly allocating hundreds of MB each frame' is therefore plausible. But the allocations are mostly the driver's buffers that Chrono requests per rebuild, not Chrono's staging list, so 'Chrono's code, not the driver' only holds for the user-space part.
3. 'Nearly half' is fair on the VM (47%) but a stretch on bare metal (38%).
4. The 92% figure covers the whole profiled run, not per frame. Calling it the driver's compiled ray-tracing code is reasonable: all the heavy threads are the driver's compute threads, and there are no JIT samples outside the frame windows.

verdicts.reasoning:
Every part of the claim holds up against the measurements and the Chrono source. I also directly tested the two things the claim said had not been measured, and both came out the way the claim predicted.

1) The measurements. Both runs (probe_2101_lp16_1024_novehicle and probe_2101_samenode_lp16_sizes) come from the same job, 422994, on the same VM (k006-004-v8), back to back.
- **Nothing moved:** 1.844–1.851 s with the vehicle hidden vs 1.968–1.998 s for the full scene.
- **Rebuilds:** with the vehicle hidden there were 0 of 3 in every regime (the first frame rebuilt, as expected). The full scene rebuilt 3 of 3 when parked and 3 of 3 when driving.
- **Main-thread CPU with the vehicle hidden:** 0.17–0.18 s per frame when parked and when driving, 0–0.02 s when nothing moved. The extra wall time is similar: 2.023 − 1.850 = 0.17 s parked, 0.20 s driving.
- **Stale or async frames ruled out:** the frame take was about 0.6 ms, and each Update burned about 28 s of worker CPU. So every Update rendered a fresh frame inside the call.
- **Where the extra time goes:** in the parked and driving frames the main thread also spent 0.03–0.04 s in the kernel, and none in the frozen ones. That fits allocating and freeing a large buffer every frame.

2) The mechanism in the source.
- Hiding the chassis clears its visual model (chrono_vehicle/ChPart.cpp:475-478). The wheel and tire only erase their own shapes (ChWheel.cpp:166-170, ChForceElementTire.cpp:139-144). The models stay behind, empty but not missing.
- The fingerprint (HashVisualModelState, ChVulkanRTScene.cpp:564-571) skips a body only if it has no model at all. Otherwise it hashes the body's pose and velocities.
- It hashes only pointers, poses and material values, never mesh vertices, so walking 21 bodies is trivial.
- When the fingerprint changes, SyncFromSystem rebuilds the whole triangle list. Each terrain triangle becomes a 576-byte record that includes a material with 8 strings, about 301 MB for 522k triangles. It then compares that list field by field with the old one (SamePrimitiveList). When they match it only stores the new fingerprint, so the revision stays put. This runs on the main thread (ChSensorManager::Update → UpdateSensors → SyncFromSystem).
- The camera is attached to the fixed terrain body, so camera motion plays no part.
- The AMD profile of the full scene shows the same functions on the main thread: FillTrianglePrimitive, material copies and string assigns.

3) New direct test, a stand-in rather than the real scene. I compiled a small C++ program against the local build's real ChVulkanRTScene::SyncFromSystem. The CPU is a Ryzen 5800X, the same generation (Zen 3) as the AMD EPYC 7V13 nodes. The scene is a 512×512 heightmap mesh (522,242 triangles, with normals and UVs) plus 20 bodies, 5 of which move.
- **5 bodies with emptied models, moved:** 0.19–0.23 s per call, revision unchanged.
- **Nothing moved:** 1–5 µs, so the fingerprint walk costs next to nothing.
- **5 bodies with no visual model at all, moved:** 0.5 µs. This supports the 'remove the vehicle bodies from the rendered system' prediction at the library level.
- **5 visible boxes, moved:** 0.70–0.74 s, with a revision bump every time.

Minor caveats, none of which overturn the claim:
- **Size of the vehicle's share:** it is noisy. In the full scene, nothing moved went from 1.976 s at the start to 1.905 s at the end of the same run, against 1.874 s hidden. The vehicle mesh is roughly 2–6% of the ray-tracing time, from only 3 frames each. That supports 'not what makes each ray expensive' but gives a loose number.
- **'Change check' wording:** it does not appear in amd/summary.json or amd/scripts/summarize.py.
- **Build version:** the AMD build's source commit can't be checked from here. Its profile's function names do match the local source.
- **'Copying':** more precisely, the list is rebuilt from the mesh, compared and freed.
- **Removing the remainder in practice:** those bodies must have no visual model at all. Setting visualization to NONE after the models exist does not do it.

A comparison against the arena heightmap can, and it is in the same file (not cited in the claim), so I reran it myself:

verdicts.reasoning:
Every cited number matches its file. The problem is how two of them are read.

1) Timings check out. On AMD at 16 threads, 1024 px, same node and back-to-back jobs (no overlap): colour+depth moving 6.612 s, static 6.699 s; depth-only moving 2.696 s, static 2.759 s. Rendering happens inside manager.Update() and take_s is only 0.7 to 10 ms, so update/take timing tricks and stale frames are ruled out. The first colour frame is 8.07 s and later frames are steady, so warm-up is excluded too. The same AMD lavapipe copied to the local Ryzen gives a similar ratio (6.16 vs 2.45 s), so node contention is not the cause either.

2) "Its tracing costs about 85 CPU-s against 28.5" needs a correction. 84.81 CPU-s is the median per 'frozen' frame (nothing moves, no rebuild) in the colour run. That run renders BOTH cameras: ChVulkanRTEngine::UpdateSensors calls each sensor's render filter one after the other in the same Update, and scene.py always keeps the depth camera. So 85 CPU-s covers colour plus depth. The colour camera alone is about 85 - 28.5 = 56 CPU-s, roughly twice the depth camera, not three times. No run with only the colour camera exists. Both runs show the same process: the worker CPU is almost all lavapipe's compiled shader code (perf: 92% [JIT]), with no rebuild in those frames. Watch out: amd/perf/perf_2101_lp16_1024_split.txt also shows 'frozen ... cpu 85.29 s', but that is 3 depth-only frames added together (3 x 28.4). The cited 84.81 is correctly from the per-frame colour probe.

3) "Rebuild is shared and paid once" is confirmed by the source and the data. GetSharedVulkanRTGpuRenderer caches one GPU renderer per (device, scene). Render() calls BuildScene only when the scene revision changes, and SyncFromSystem runs once per UpdateSensors. So the first sensor rebuilds and the second finds the same revision. Both cameras also write one 32-bit word per pixel, so the output buffer is never reallocated. Measured: main-thread CPU for a moving frame is 0.70 s in both runs; worker CPU is the same with or without a rebuild. The rebuild's extra wall time is 0.92 s (colour) vs 0.82 s (depth) from the probe, and 0.77 vs 0.78 s from the harness minus the probe's frozen median. The 0.1 s gap is noise, so "about 0.8-0.9 s, the same either way" is the fair statement.

4) The "cheap elsewhere" framing overstates it. The raygen shader shows the colour pipeline traces a primary ray plus a shadow ray toward the directional light, evaluates the material, and may add a reflection ray. Depth traces one ray. Colour should therefore cost about 2x depth on any backend, and it does on the others too. On local Mesa 25.2.8, a depth trace alone (no rebuild) is 0.063 s and colour adds +0.13 to +0.24 s. With OptiX, depth-only is 6.9 to 7.3 ms against 17.5 to 25.2 ms with colour. So colour is "cheap" there only in absolute seconds. Nothing about colour is specific to Mesa 24.2.8. All tracing on the AMD Mesa build is about 25x slower (trace-only depth: 1.67 s vs 0.063 s on the same Ryzen), and colour's roughly 2x multiple of that becomes seconds.

5) The small numbers depend on the regime. "+0.14 s" on local Mesa 25.2.8 is the static difference (1.347 vs 1.213 s). The moving difference is +0.24 s (1.361 vs 1.122 s), pooled about +0.17 s, from only 5 frames each; the depth run itself scatters 1.10 to 1.26 s. The 5090 figure of +0.07 s holds in both regimes over 30 frames. But the GPU depth trace alone takes 4 ms, so that +0.07 s is copy/submit overhead, not tracing. The OptiX 17.5 ms (moving) and 25.2 ms (tight) are correct and cover both cameras. The tap checks the launch counter, and the OptiX access filter finishes the GPU-to-host copy before publishing the buffer, so these are not stale frames.

verdicts.reasoning:
The Vulkan half of the claim holds. The OptiX half does not hold as worded.

Vulkan (holds). The Chrono source matches the claim. ChSensorManager::Update calls ChVulkanRTEngine::UpdateSensors directly, with no worker thread. For each due sensor that call runs every filter's Apply in order. The render filter records the trace and a staging copy, then submits and blocks until the work is done (EndSubmitWait, ChFilterVulkanRTRender.cpp:2141-2150, called at 3212). It then copies the result into the host buffer (CopyOutputToHost). The access filter for the Vulkan-only build (ChFilterAccess.cpp:501-626) does a plain host copy, also inside Update. The build notes (vulkan_local/build_provenance.json) say the AMD build's sensor source is identical to /home/harry/chrono, and a diff against the mirror copy showed no differences. So by the time take() starts, the frame is already sitting in memory. take() then does three things: hands the buffer to the caller (GetBuffer), creates a no-copy numpy view (ARGOUTVIEW typemap), and makes one flipped copy. The harness's frame counter check would raise an error on a skipped or stale frame.

The measurements agree. On AMD, the depth-only take medians are 0.19-0.79 ms against updates of 0.87-29.5 s. With colour the take is 10.5 ms against 6.6 s. A local numpy test of the flipped copies gave about 0.1-0.3 ms for 1024 depth and 5.4 ms for 1024 colour, in line with those numbers. One small error: the quoted upper bound of 1.2 ms (0.00121 s) does not appear in amd/summary.json. The largest depth-only median there is 0.79 ms, and single frames reach 2.1 ms.

OptiX (does not hold as worded). The 4096 numbers are right: update 66.7 ms, take 32.3 ms, total median 98.9 ms. Two parts are wrong:

1. "Matters only at very large sizes" is contradicted by the project's own OptiX files:
   - Depth-only at 1024: take is 1.5 of 7.3 ms (about 20%).
   - Depth-only at 2048: 4.6 of 24.9 ms moving, 7.6 of 26.3 ms static.
   - With colour at 1024 (optix5090_rgbd.json): take is 7.6 of 18.1 ms moving (42%) and 15.4 of 25.1 ms static (61%).
   In absolute terms these are small, but as a share of the frame the collection step matters at every size of 1024 and up, and most of all with colour.

2. At 4096 the take is not just a copy. With OptiX, ChFilterAccess<Depth>::Apply gets a new page-locked (pinned) host buffer every frame, because GetBuffer moves the buffer out to the user and the drained lag buffer is never recycled. So each take also frees the previous frame's page-locked buffer.
   - Local micro-tests with CUDA 13.2 at 4096: freeing a 67 MB page-locked buffer takes about 10.4 ms, the numpy flipped copy about 10 ms, and allocating the buffer about 31 ms.
   - The stored data backs this up. The first frame's take, which has no previous buffer to free, is 21 ms against 32 ms in steady state. That 11 ms gap matches the free time. The gaps are 2.8 ms against a 2.6 ms free at 2048, and 1.1 ms against 0.7 ms at 1024.
   - So roughly a third of the 32 ms is buffer release, not copying. By the same logic, about 31 ms of the 67 ms update is probably allocating page-locked memory rather than rendering.
   - One oddity is unexplained: in the static runs the take jumps partway through (4.2 to 7.5 ms at 2048, 7.5 to 15.5 ms with colour). The saved per-frame data cannot rule out some waiting in those frames.

None of this changes the main conclusion for AMD: collecting the frame is under 1% of the per-frame cost there.

verdicts.reasoning:
Most of the numbers check out. The explanation is wrong or loose in three places.

What holds:
1. AMD numbers. On the virtual machine at 1024, the first frame took 4.689 s against a later-frame median of 2.696 s. On bare metal at 1024 it was 3.269 vs 2.294 s, and at 256 it was 2.297 vs 0.872 s. Scene build ranged from 0.416 to 0.715 s. Across all 14 AMD runs the first-frame extra was 0.94 to 1.99 s, so "1-2 s" is roughly right; the three bare-metal runs at 32 to 128 threads came in just under 1 s.
2. The AMD cache really was warm. No first frame came near 60-77 s. The probe on the same node lists a Mesa disk-cache thread ("python:disk$N"). The extra hardly changes with thread count (about 1.5 s at 1 thread, 2.0 s at 16), which points to single-threaded pipeline setup rather than rendering.
3. The local cold-cache runs really were cold. For the Mesa 25.2.8 run, run_all.sh deletes the cache folder first. For AMD's Mesa, the cache folder's creation time (16:23:48.747) matches the start of that run in run_all.log.
4. The mechanism fits the code. Chrono builds the ray-tracing pipeline lazily, on the first render (ChVulkanRTGpuRenderer constructor, vkCreateRayTracingPipelinesKHR, called with no pipeline cache). In Mesa, llvmpipe's generate_variant looks up and stores the compiled shader in the disk cache (lp_disk_cache_find_shader / insert_shader).
5. Timing is not stale or async. The Vulkan path renders synchronously inside manager.Update (take_s is under 1 ms), and the harness's take waits for a new launch count, so no old frame is reused.
6. The ~77 s figure is real but was never measured here. env.sh line 25-26 says: "without a shared cache every process pays a ~77 s LLVM compile on first render instead of ~0.8 s".

What needs correcting:
(a) OptiX does not compile "once per process". ChOptixEngine creates a ChOptixPipeline, whose CompileBaseShaders runs NVRTC with nothing cached, so the compile happens once per sensor manager, i.e. every scene build. The OptiX log shows "Shader compile time" five times (8.15-8.19 s) in one process, once per image size. Also, the 8.5-8.9 s is the whole scene build; the compile alone is 8.15-8.37 s.
(b) The lavapipe first-frame extra is likewise paid once per scene, not once per process. In one process, lvp16_depth paid about 1.3 s again for each size, and amdlvp16_depth_small paid about 1.0 s again for its second size. In practice nav_runner.py builds one scene per mission run, so "once" holds there.
(c) The 63 s and 31 s are whole first frames, not compile time alone. Each includes one normal render (2.46 s at 1024, 1.18 s at 256) plus the roughly 1 s warm-cache extra. The compile itself is about 60 s and about 28 s. The two runs also used different image sizes (1024 vs 256).
(d) Minor points:
- The OptiX "29-45 ms" counts only the Update call for sizes 256-2048; including the frame copy it is 28.6-46.3 ms. At 4096 it is 93/114 ms, and depth plus colour at 1024 is 61 ms.
- The cited "problems" list does not exist in amd/summary.json, which has only harness_rows and probe_only_rows.
- The claim's check command fails with KeyError 'scene_build_s' on the OptiX JSON; the key name for the Vulkan table is fine.
- Cache warmth on AMD is inferred from the timings; no cache hits were actually recorded.

With a warm Mesa shader cache, the first AMD frame is about 1-2 s slower than later frames: 4.69 vs 2.70 s at 1024 on the virtual machine, 3.27 vs 2.29 s on bare metal at 16 threads (about 0.95 s extra at 32-128 threads), and 2.30 vs 0.87 s at 256. The extra barely depends on thread count, which fits one-off pipeline setup rather than rendering. Scene build takes 0.42-0.72 s. With an empty cache, the whole first frame took 63 s with AMD's Mesa 24.2.8 at 1024 and 31 s with Mesa 25.2.8 at 256, both measured locally. Removing the normal render and the warm-cache extra from each leaves roughly 60 s and 28 s of pipeline compile. Cold cache was not re-tested on AMD; the ~77 s figure comes only from a comment in env.sh. OptiX recompiles its shaders (8.15-8.37 s, inside an 8.5-8.9 s scene build) every time a sensor manager is created, not once per process. Its first frame then takes about 29-46 ms at 256-2048 (93-114 ms at 4096).

verdicts.reasoning:
Every number in the claim matches the raw files, and the back-projection timings came out the same when I re-ran them. The problem is how two of the numbers are framed.

What checks out:
- **Height-grid conversion time.** backprojection_timing.json (host luffy, Ryzen 7 5800X, numpy 1.26.4, 30 repeats) gives medians of 55.68 ms (AMD frame with colour), 55.85 ms (OptiX frame with colour) and 53.96 ms (OptiX frame with an all-zero colour image). Recomputing the medians from the `all_s` lists gives the same values. My own run of the same code, 8 repeats, gave 56.2, 56.2 and 54.4 ms, plus 55.2 ms for the depth-only OptiX frame.
- **88% of the sensing step.** The depth render median in sustained_depth_1024.json is 6.93 ms. 53.96 / (53.96 + 6.93) = 88.6%, and with colour it is about 89%. The 88% and ~61 ms figures hold.
- **Stage breakdown.** Colour averaging is 10.17 ms and the ray grid (mgrid plus secant) is 11.35 ms. The stages add up to 52.1 ms against the 55.7 ms total, which is consistent. My re-run gave 10.5 and 11.4 ms on the AMD frame, and 10.8 and 12.1 ms on the all-zero image.
- **The depth-only runner really feeds an all-zero image.** scripts/nav_runner.py line 134 builds `blank_rgb = np.zeros(...)`, and line 139 passes it to `nav.observe`, which calls `grid_from_arrays`. The colour sums over zeros cost the same as over real colours. Converting the zero image to float64 adds another ~1.7 ms, so colour costs this runner slightly more than 10 ms.
- **Ray grid recomputed every call.** sensor_map_v2.py line 43 computes the focal length and line 44 calls `np.mgrid` on every call, even though the camera never changes. In a quick test, reusing a precomputed ray grid saved about 12 ms.
- **Driving-loop numbers.** In the moving regime, `physics_between_median_s` is 47.51 ms and `loop_fps_including_physics` is 17.89. The loop took 16.77 s for 300 frames, i.e. 55.9 ms per frame, and render plus physics medians add to 54.4 ms. The 144.3 fps is render-only (1 / 6.93 ms).

What needs qualifying:
1. **The 17.9 fps loop leaves out the conversion.** sustained_loop.py only steps physics, calls `manager.Update` and takes the depth frame; it never back-projects or plans. "The whole loop" therefore means render plus physics. If the ~54 ms conversion ran every frame, the loop would drop to about 9 fps (1 / (55.9 + 54) ms).
2. **The ~61 ms step was never measured as one step.** It adds the render time (one process, on the GPU) to the conversion time (a separate CPU-only script). `observe()` also does extra work each decision that the ~61 ms leaves out: a valid-depth fraction and grid publishing (`V2.set_grid`).
3. **The 25 physics steps are a benchmark choice.** 25 steps of 2 ms is 0.05 s of simulated time, about 1.9 ms of wall time per step, so physics runs at roughly real time. It is time the simulation must spend anyway, not a slowdown in the sensing pipeline. The real runner renders once per planning decision (1-2 Hz or once per waypoint), not every 25 steps. Comparing 17.9 fps with 144 fps compares different things.
4. **The 47.5 ms is not purely those 25 steps.** In the tight regime a single physics step took 5.27 ms, against ~1.9 ms per step on average. That points to a fixed ~3.4 ms per-frame overhead folded into the "physics" time.
5. **Timing noise.** Only the colour-image frame got a stage breakdown in the cited file, so the all-zero-image breakdown above is my own measurement. Other processes were running during my re-run, and one repeat came out at 62 ms, so treat single timings as ±5% noise.

verdicts.corrected_claim: With OptiX, a 1024x1024 depth render takes about 7 ms, and the CPU conversion from depth frame to planner height grid (54-56 ms on the Ryzen 7 5800X) becomes the main cost of a sensing step. That is about 88% of a ~61 ms render-plus-conversion step, a figure added up from two separate measurements. Inside the conversion, about 10 ms goes to averaging the three colour channels, which the depth-only runner still pays because it passes an all-zero colour image. Another ~11 ms rebuilds the per-pixel ray grid, which never changes. Separately, in the benchmark's driving loop the 25 physics steps between frames (0.05 s of simulated time, roughly real time) took 47.5 ms, so the render-plus-physics loop ran at 17.9 fps against 144 fps for rendering alone. That loop did not include the height-grid conversion; running it every frame would bring the loop to about 9 fps. The real runner renders once per planning decision, not every 25 steps.

verdicts.reasoning:
The numbers and the two code explanations hold up. The claim goes wrong where it joins them into one story about the loop.

What checks out:
1. Every cited figure matches the JSON files. Grid conversion medians are 55.7, 55.8 and 54.0 ms. Colour averaging is 10.2 ms and the ray grid 11.3 ms. Physics between frames is 47.5 ms, the loop ran at 17.89 fps, and rendering alone at 144 fps. The share works out: 54.0 / (54.0 + 6.9) is 88.6%.
2. The code does what the claim says. sensor_map_v2.grid_from_arrays rebuilds the pixel grid, rays and secant on every call (lines 43-47). It averages all three colour channels (line 61), and nav_runner.py passes an all-zero uint8 image when colour is off (lines 134 and 139). The depth-only models read no colour (their channels are range_abs, sec1, speed, valid), so that work is wasted.
3. My own quick runs agree. On the depth-only input (OptiX depth plus the zero image), colour averaging still costs 10.2 ms and the ray grid 12.9 ms. Caching the ray grid saves 12.8 ms and gives an identical height grid. Skipping colour saves about 11 ms more. So colour costs slightly more than 10 ms in total, because converting the zero image to float64 is also paid.

What needs qualifying:
(a) The 17.9 fps loop never ran the grid conversion. It covered physics, rendering and about 1.5 ms per frame of a freshness check: 1/17.89 is 55.9 ms, against 47.5 + 6.9 = 54.4 ms. Saying "another 47.5 ms ... so the whole loop ran at 17.9 fps" right after the 54-56 ms figure mixes two different loops. With the conversion on every frame, the loop would take about 110 ms, roughly 9 fps.
(b) Rendering every 25 physics steps (one 50 ms control interval) was the test's choice. The real runner renders once per planning decision, every 0.5-2 s of simulated time. Physics takes 47.5 ms per 50 ms simulated, about 0.95 times real time, so it caps the loop near real time however fast rendering is. Setting 17.9 fps against 144 compares a full loop with rendering alone.
(c) The "~61 ms sensing step" was not measured. It adds two numbers from separate scripts. observe() does about 1 ms of extra work, which is negligible.
(d) The claim says the next limits are "elsewhere" but leaves out the planner, the largest cost per decision. The stored benchmark (nav_v1/bench_cpu.json and bench_cuda.json, AMD node) splits a decision into:
   - proposing candidates: 128 ms
   - corridor extraction: 182 ms
   - scoring: 42 ms on GPU, 335 ms on CPU
   - grid conversion: 66-68 ms
   Only for the sensing step itself is the grid conversion the next limit.
(e) Physics timing depends on the vehicle's state and may be muddied by other effects:
   - A single step right after a frame took 5.27 ms in the back-to-back run, against 1.9 ms per step in the 25-step run.
   - The shared harness measured 1.5-2.3 ms per step while moving, and single parked steps jumped from 1.56 to 3.4 ms midway through a run.
   - The CPU frequency governor is schedutil, which adjusts speed with load.
   About 3 ms per frame of what is booked as physics could be render aftermath or a CPU slowdown. The source argues against aftermath: the render thread's only work after the depth filter publishes the frame is a CUDA sync and a notify. I could not tell these apart without running Chrono again. The 17.9 fps wall-clock figure is not affected, but the 47.5 / 7 ms split is less certain than stated.
(f) The 54-56 ms is from luffy's Ryzen with numpy 1.26. On the AMD node the same step took 66-68 ms.

Minor: the "HOW TO CHECK" rerun command leaves out the required --out argument.

verdicts.reasoning:
I recomputed every number from the raw files. The facts in the claim hold up. What the claim leaves out is that the local test shows a much bigger slowdown than the one it is used to explain.

What checks out:
- **Local four-at-once test.** I recomputed the medians from the per-frame times. The four runs sat still at 7.641, 7.687, 7.688 and 7.775 s per frame (7.58-7.64 s while moving). One run alone took 2.450 s, so the four runs were 3.12-3.17x slower (3.14x at the median). The four runs started together and finished within the same second, so they really did overlap. Nothing from the separate OptiX investigation was running at that time. The newer local Mesa showed the same kind of slowdown: 3.28-3.71 s against 1.213 s alone (2.7-3.05x).
- **AMD thread counts.** At 8 threads the moving median is 4.581 s (4.653 s static). At 4 threads it is 8.430 s (8.467 s static). I recomputed both from the per-frame times.
- **No shared-node runs on AMD.** Every AMD script runs one measurement after another. Each job asked for 16 CPUs, and each mi2101x node is a 16-CPU virtual machine (EPYC 7V13, one thread per core), so each job had the whole machine. The job logs confirm that jobs landing on the same node never overlapped: task 7 on k006-004-v8 ended at 16:21:22 and the extras job started there at 16:21:43; task 6 on k006-005-v4 ended at 16:15:37 and task 8 started at 16:18:32.
- **Source reading.** lp_screen.c lines 1171-1175 are as quoted, and LP_MAX_THREADS is 32. The CPU count comes from sched_getaffinity in u_cpu_detect.c, so it follows the CPUs a process may use. One correction: lavapipe starts two pools of that size, one for rasterising and one for compute (lp_screen.c 1091 and 1097). That matches the AMD thread counts: 5, 11, 19, 35 and 67 threads for 1, 4, 8, 16 and 32 or more lavapipe threads. An earlier render audit also found that nrd_use_lavapipe leaves LP_NUM_THREADS unset.

Needed qualifications:
1. **The local test overshoots by about 2x.** 4.3-4.6 s against 2.6 s is only 1.65-1.77x slower, but the local test shows 3.1x. Four runs rendering at the same moment on a 16-CPU node would each get about 4 CPUs, which the AMD data put at 8.43 s or worse, not 4.3-4.6 s. The observed figure instead matches one run with 8 threads (4.58 s), as if each run got about half the node. That fits renders that only partly overlap, since each decision also spends about 1.7 s planning. It does not need the full-pool oversubscription the claim describes. AMD's own data show oversubscription is cheap there: at 512 px on one node, 32 threads on 16 CPUs took 1.376 s against 1.213 s at 16 threads, only 13% slower. So calling it "the same effect" is overstated. Only the direction matches.
2. **The machines differ.** The local machine is a Ryzen 7 5800X with 8 cores and 16 hyperthreads. The AMD node is a 16-CPU virtual machine, and "dedicated" means the whole virtual machine, not the whole physical server.
3. **I cannot find where 4.3-4.6 s comes from in the saved records.** In the nav_v1 campaign (120 runs; RUNNING.md says one worker per shard), each run's median render time was 2.35-3.46 s. The 4.2-4.4 s figures there are the median time for a whole decision (render plus planning), not the render. The 4.3-4.6 s render figure may be a mix-up of the two.
4. **The quoted wording cannot be checked.** Neither "the same effect" nor "consistent with, but not proof" appears in any saved file. run_followup.sh only calls the four-at-once test "the AMD 'four runs share a node' situation".

verdicts.corrected_claim: No render_latency_v1 AMD job ran more than one render at a time on a node, so the shared-node slowdown was never reproduced there. Locally, four simultaneous runs of AMD's Mesa at 16 threads each, on 8 cores with hyperthreading, took 7.64-7.78 s per frame, 3.1x one run alone (2.45 s). That is about twice the 1.65-1.77x slowdown (2.6 s to 4.3-4.6 s) it is meant to explain. On a whole 16-CPU AMD node, one run takes 2.70 s at 16 threads, 4.58 s at 8 and 8.43 s at 4. The shared-node figure matches each run getting about half the node, which fits renders that only partly overlap. It does not need a big oversubscription penalty: on AMD, 32 threads on 16 CPUs cost only about 13%. By default lavapipe sizes two thread pools to the CPUs a process may use (capped at 32), and the project's lavapipe setup leaves LP_NUM_THREADS unset, so each shared-node run would start full pools. The local test shows a slowdown in the same direction, not the same size. The render origin of the 4.3-4.6 s figure is also unconfirmed: the nav_v1 campaign's render medians were 2.35-3.46 s per run, and its 4.2-4.4 s figures are whole-decision times. The proper test is still four simultaneous runs on one mi2101x node, with and without LP_NUM_THREADS=4 plus CPU binding.

verdicts.reasoning:
The numbers and the source reading are right. What the claim leaves out is the AMD evidence that bears on the four-runs-on-one-node story, and that evidence does not support it.

What checks out:
1. Local results (vulkan_local/summary_table.json). Four simultaneous runs of AMD's Mesa at 16 threads had static medians of 7.641, 7.686, 7.688 and 7.775 s. One run alone took 2.450 s, so the ratio is about 3.1x. The machine is a Ryzen 7 5800X with 8 physical cores and 16 hardware threads. run_followup.sh started the four with & and wait, and they did overlap.
2. AMD results. At 8 threads the moving median is 4.581 s; at 4 threads it is 8.430 s.
3. The AMD benchmark jobs ran one render process per job, one after another. The scripts contain no &, wait or srun fan-out.
4. Mesa source. lp_screen.c lines 1171-1175 set the thread count to nr_cpus, let LP_NUM_THREADS override it, and cap it at 32. u_cpu_detect.c counts nr_cpus from the CPU affinity mask, so 'CPUs it is allowed to use' is correct.

Problems:
(a) Four runs on one node were measured on AMD, in the nav_v1 production campaign, and the render did not slow down.
- Missions 0-12 were job 421779, submitted with NAV_WORKERS=4 (confirmed with sacct).
- They ran on mi2104x nodes that were allocated whole (128 CPUs), with LP_NUM_THREADS=16 set in the job script.
- Shard 0 finished in 377 s, while its four arms took 106+278+275+358 s. Preserved file times also show all four starting together, so the arms ran at the same time.
- Median render per run was 2.35-2.59 s.
- Missions 13-29 ran one arm at a time on 16-CPU mi2101x nodes and rendered in 2.53-3.46 s.
- Caveat: those shared nodes had 128 CPUs, so this is not a test of four runs packed onto a 16-CPU mi2101x node. That specific case was indeed never run.

(b) No stored AMD render comes near 4.3-4.6 s because of node sharing. I looked at nav_v1 main, main_nocap, rand, video and the pilot logs.
- The closest is a single depth-only pilot (job 421529, alone on its own node, LP_NUM_THREADS=8 per the current nav_pilot.sbatch). Its renders took 4.56-4.90 s, matching the 8-thread benchmark.
- The whole decision time (render plus back-projection plus planning) is 4.26-4.40 s median per arm (nav_v1 REPORT.md), and 4.30 s median across all runs.
- So the 4.3-4.6 s figure may be the whole decision time or the 8-thread pilot, not four runs rendering at once. Its source should be pinned down before any mechanism is argued.

(c) The local test cannot tell 'every run starts a full thread pool' apart from 'four runs simply share the CPU'.
- It set LP_NUM_THREADS=16 explicitly, so it never exercised the default thread count.
- It rendered back to back, so the four runs overlapped 100% of the time. In the real loop, rendering is only about 55-60% of each decision.
- Oversubscription did not waste total work. Four runs produced 4/7.69 = 0.52 frames/s combined, against 0.41 frames/s for one run alone. Only involuntary context switches rose (246,875 vs 10,356).
- The size doesn't match either. A 3.1x slowdown applied to AMD's 2.70 s single-run render predicts about 8.4 s, but the observation is about 1.7x.
- Four fully overlapping renders on 16 CPUs should each take about the 4-thread time (8.43 s). A result of 4.3-4.6 s is faster than that, which points to partial overlap rather than oversubscription loss. Calling the local result 'the same effect' is too strong.

(d) A small point: in the real campaign, nav_run.sbatch and nav_run32.sbatch export LP_NUM_THREADS=16. So LP_NUM_THREADS did not 'limit' the thread pool there. It fixed it at the full count.

verdicts.corrected_claim:
No controlled benchmark ran several renders on one AMD node: every job under render_latency_v1/amd rendered in a single process. But the nav_v1 campaign did run four arms at once on one node (mi2104x, all 128 CPUs allocated, LP_NUM_THREADS=16), and renders stayed at 2.35-2.59 s median. No stored AMD log shows a 4.3-4.6 s render caused by sharing a node. The nearest matches are the whole planning decision (render plus planning, 4.26-4.40 s median) and a depth-only pilot run alone at LP_NUM_THREADS=8 (4.56-4.90 s). The source of the 4.3-4.6 s figure needs to be pinned down first.

Locally, four simultaneous runs at 16 threads each on the 8-core, 16-thread CPU took 7.64-7.78 s against 2.45 s for one run alone (3.1x). That was a worst case: back-to-back rendering with the thread count forced. Combined output was still higher than one run alone (0.52 vs 0.41 frames/s), so the test cannot separate 'every run starts a full thread pool' from plain CPU sharing. It also predicts about 8.4 s on AMD, not 4.3-4.6 s.

Mesa does start one worker per CPU in the affinity mask (capped at 32) unless LP_NUM_THREADS is set. The nav jobs set LP_NUM_THREADS=16, so it fixed the pool at full size rather than limiting it. Four runs on a single 16-CPU mi2101x node remain untested.

verdicts.reasoning:
I recomputed every cited number from the raw files, and they all match. What needs fixing is how two of them are worded.

Numbers recomputed from the per-frame lists in vulkan_local/*.json (5 frames each):
- Mesa 25.2.8, 16 threads, static median: 1.162 / 1.180 / 1.213 s at 256 / 512 / 1024.
- 1024 at 4 / 8 threads: 1.377 / 1.211 s.
- Breakdown files: worker-thread CPU per rebuild frame is 6.41 CPU-s at 1024 and 6.07 at 256. A frame where nothing moved takes 0.0632 s at 1024 (median of 6 frames).
- Every local 25.2.8 log shows llvmpipe on LLVM 20.1.2, and the installed package is mesa-vulkan-drivers 25.2.8.
- Every AMD cluster log shows Mesa 24.2.8, so a newer Mesa really has not been tried on the EPYC nodes.

Source checks:
- In 24.2.8, lvp_execute.c lines 4487-4492 call the builder directly, and lvp_acceleration_structure.c has no threads at all. Its builder just splits the triangle list in half in input order. That makes it cheap to build but a poor tree to trace.
- The data agree. With 24.2.8 a rebuild adds only 0.305 s and no extra worker-thread CPU, while tracing alone takes 1.67 s.
- I downloaded the 25.2.8 file (outside the project, to /tmp). It is a completely different builder: Vulkan's shared build path, with a radix sort and compute-shader dispatches that run on llvmpipe's worker threads. So "the 24.2.8 source reading does not carry over" and "the cost is spread over worker threads" are both backed by the source.

Qualifications:
1. "Dominated by the rebuild" only holds if Chrono's own scene work counts as part of the rebuild. The 1.21 s frame breaks down as:
   - about 0.50 s of Chrono copying and comparing the scene on the main thread;
   - about 0.20 s of main-thread flatten and upload;
   - about 0.46 s of lavapipe building the search structure;
   - 0.06 s of tracing.
   So the search-structure build itself is only about 38% of the frame. The roughly 0.7 s of Chrono-side work happens on any backend: the RTX 5090 frame is 0.69 s. A Mesa upgrade cannot remove it.
2. The 6.4 CPU-s includes about 0.7 CPU-s of tracing, which is what the nothing-moved frame uses. The build alone is about 5.7 CPU-s at 1024 and 6.0 at 256. It is still roughly independent of image size.
3. The claim that threads hardly matter was measured on an 8-core Ryzen 5800X with 2 threads per core, so 8 vs 16 threads says little. Also, 5.7 CPU-s of work would need at least 1.4 s on 4 threads, yet the whole 4-thread frame took 1.38 s. Either the CPU-s figure overstates the real work (shared cores, overhead) or LP_NUM_THREADS does not cap the builder. The 4-thread run recorded no per-thread CPU, so we cannot tell which.
4. The breakdown runs use only 3 frames per case, though the spread is small.
5. The "roughly halve" projection is correctly called untested. It assumes the Chrono-side 0.7 s behaves the same on EPYC, which has not been checked.

verdicts.corrected_claim: Mesa 25.2.8 spends a frame's time very differently from 24.2.8, because 25.2.8 replaced the lavapipe builder with Vulkan's shared compute-shader builder. The reading of the 24.2.8 source does not carry over. On the local Ryzen (8 cores, 2 threads per core), a 25.2.8 frame costs 1.16 / 1.18 / 1.21 s at 256 / 512 / 1024 and 1.38 / 1.21 / 1.21 s at 4 / 8 / 16 threads. Almost all of it is work caused by the scene changing: about 0.5 s of Chrono copying the scene plus 0.2 s of main-thread flattening and upload (both the same on any backend, since the RTX 5090 frame is 0.69 s), about 0.46 s of lavapipe building its search structure, and only 0.06 s of tracing. That build uses about 5.7-6.0 CPU-s (6.4 at 1024 including tracing) spread over the worker threads, whatever the image size. Since 4 threads are barely slower, that CPU figure overstates the real work. The 24.2.8 builder is single-threaded and trivial, so its rebuild adds only about 0.3 s, and its cost sits in the 1.67 s trace. The idea that upgrading Mesa would roughly halve the AMD render time comes from the local Ryzen only and has not been tested on the EPYC nodes.

verdicts.reasoning:
Most of the claim holds up. All the numbers match the files. The two Mesa versions really do build the search structure differently. But three parts of the explanation go further than the evidence.

What holds:
- The frame times are correct: 1.162 / 1.180 / 1.213 s at 256 / 512 / 1024, and 1.377 / 1.211 / 1.213 s at 4 / 8 / 16 threads. The per-frame spread is about 0.1 s.
- The per-frame breakdown matches: 6.41 CPU-s at 1024 versus 6.07 at 256. A frame where nothing moved takes 0.063 s.
- The two drivers really are Mesa 24.2.8 (with LLVM 19.1.7) and 25.2.8 (with LLVM 20.1.2).
- The frame is finished inside the update call; collecting it afterwards takes about 0.0004 s. So the frame arriving late, or an old frame being reused, cannot explain the numbers. A cold shader cache gave the same result (1.178 s).
- In 24.2.8 the tree builder is one plain routine run inline when the command buffer executes, with no threads, as the claim says. It just halves the triangle list in its input order.
- I fetched the 25.2.8 source from the Mesa site. That routine was replaced by Mesa's shared builder: it sorts the triangles by spatial position and then clusters them. This runs as compute jobs on the pool whose size is set by LP_NUM_THREADS (no busy-waiting). Chrono asks for a fast-to-trace structure and does not allow updates, and in that case the shared builder picks the clustering method (PLOC). So "spread over worker threads" is backed by the source, not just by the CPU accounting.
- The "halve" projection really is untested: every AMD run used Mesa 24.2.8.

What needs qualifying:

1. "Dominated by the rebuild" is only true if "rebuild" includes Chrono's own work. Of the 1.21 s frame:
   - about 0.50 s is Chrono copying the scene every frame, on the main thread;
   - about 0.2 s is flattening the triangles and uploading them, also on the main thread;
   - only about 0.45–0.5 s is Mesa building the search structure (update 0.727 s, minus 0.063 s of tracing, minus about 0.2 s of main-thread work);
   - tracing is 0.063 s.
   The Chrono part is still there on a real GPU: the RTX 5090 Vulkan run takes 0.694 s per frame at 1024, and its scene copy alone is 0.485 s. So much of the insensitivity to image size and threads comes from Chrono's single-threaded work, not from Mesa. Mesa's own build is only about 40% of the frame.

2. The "about 6.4 CPU-s" figure needs three caveats:
   - It is all worker-thread CPU during the update, tracing included (0.71 CPU-s at 1024), so the build alone is about 5.7–6.0 CPU-s.
   - It was measured on a Ryzen 7 5800X with 8 physical cores and 16 hardware threads, which inflates CPU-seconds. That also means 8 and 16 threads giving the same time says little.
   - With 4 threads the whole frame is only 0.17 s slower, and slower tracing accounts for much of that. So the build finishes in roughly the same ~0.45 s on 4 workers, using at most about 2 CPU-s. Most of the ~6 CPU-s at 16 threads is thread-count overhead, not work the build needs. It should not be read as the build's cost. (No CPU-time figures exist for the 4- and 8-thread runs, so this is inferred from wall time.)

3. The comparison mixes more than one change. The builds differ in LLVM version and packaging (Ubuntu package versus the cluster build), not just the Mesa version. The builder change is the likely cause, but it was not isolated.
   Also, the 24.2.8 build itself is cheap: update 1.98 s minus 1.67 s tracing minus 0.21 s main-thread work leaves about 0.1 s. Its slowness comes from tracing through a poorly organised tree. Contrasting it as "single-threaded" is accurate but is not why 24.2.8 is slow.
